speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONFINEMENT OF CONVICT PENDING DETERMINATION OF HIS APPEAL
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice and to call to his attention a comment made yesterday by the Chief Justice of Ontario in the appeal court of that province in which he stated that it did not seem to be in the interest of public security to keep men sentenced to penitentiary in local gaols. In view of the recent escape from the Don gaol in Toronto, will the minister give consideration to reviewing section 49, subsection 2, of the Penitentiary Act with a view to meeting the situation mentioned by the Chief Justice?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I thank the leader of the opposition for calling my attention to this comment of the Chief Justice of Ontario. Of course, men sentenced to penitentiary are kept in local gaols only during the time when they are entitled to appeal from the sentence to penitentiary, but the question whether or not, even during that time, they should be left in the local gaols will be inquired into by the officers of the department. It must be realized that there would be inconvenience in moving to the penitentiary during that period prisoners whose sentence to penitentiary has not become definite. However, the advantages and disadvantages will be given careful consideration.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRESENT POSITION AS TO GASOLINE AND FUELS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRESENT POSITION AS TO GASOLINE AND FUELS
speechtext:
Some weeks ago the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) asked me to give the house a complete outline of the present fuel position. I undertook to do so,
100- 250
and accordingly, I will now give the statement on the position of petroleum products, both gasoline and fuels. I have delayed making this statement to observe the effect of the invasion of Europe, which was launched on June 6, and the effect on Canada as far as the supply and consumption of petroleum products are concerned. The Canadian position is affected chiefly in the matter of aviation and motor gasolines.
Our position at this moment may be summed up as follows: If the allies are able to win a reasonably quick overpowering victory, our position will probably not deteriorate to the point of further curtailment, due entirely to the conservation measures we have introduced and enforced. If, however, the invasion should develop into' a long bitter struggle, there is a probability that we may all have to do with less gasoline in Canada. Our only possible course is to continue to conserve every possible gallon of gasoline. Needless consumption of gasoline robs our fighting men of the fuel they will require for their planes and motorized equipment, and that we cannot permit.
I would ask you to note that the total consumption of gasoline in Canada includes aviation gasoline, the consumption of which has necessarily risen to staggering proportions. And it is this increase, with other war essentials, which has been responsible for any increased consumption shown. None of us can quarrel with any quantity of gasoline properly used for such purposes.
I will now state the position with regard to motor gasoline, and for purposes of comparison I will deal with the four yearly periods each ending on March 31, for the years 1941 to 1944 inclusive.
Motor gasoline consumption in Canada in these periods for all purposes including the armed services, the Alaska highway, agricultural, and other war essentials, was as follows: Year ended
March 31	Gallons
1941		 882,216,930
1942		 944,178,060
1943		 787,710,630
1944		 814,248,820
It must be borne in mind that in these four years we had the great growth in our war effort. We had to service the trucks and equipment for the construction of over one hundred and twenty additional airports for the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F., many far removed from rail head. Also, the trucks and equipment for the construction of the Alaska highway and a greatly increased truck haulage of materials from our widely scattered war plants.
We had to meet ever increasing demands of the armed forces and other essential uses iden-

Petroleum Products

tified with the war. We took care of all of these demands and at the same time reduced the consumption of motor gasoline slightly under the consumption for the year 1939 which totalled 824,997,390 gallons.
Motor gasoline consumption was increasing rapidly in the immediate pre-war years, and on the basis of the percentage increase which was current in those years, we estimate that motor gasoline consumption for the year ended March 31, 1942, would have exceeded 980,000,000 gallons had it not been for the voluntary conservation campaign which was launched in 1941.
In the year ended March 31, 1943-the first ration year-motor	gasoline consumption
totalled 787,710,630 gallons, or 156,467,430 gallons less than the actual consumption of the previous twelve months, and 192,289,370 gallons less than the estimated consumption of 980,000,000 gallons to which I have just referred.
While motor gasoline consumption at the close of the second year of rationing showed an increase of 26,538,190 gallons over the year ended March 31, 1943, direct sales to the armed forces and sales of marked gasoline used chiefly in agricultural machinery increased by
10.640.000	gallons and 30,940,000 gallons respectively. There was, therefore, an actual decline in consumption of motor gasoline during the second complete year of gasoline rationing of 15,050,000 gallons.
If we assume that consumption for the years ended March 31, 1943, and March 31, 1944, would have reached at least 980,000,000 gallons-which is the actual indicated consumption for the year ended March 31, 1942- the voluntary appeal and two full years of gasoline rationing have effected a total saving of approximately 393,750,000 gallons of motor gasoline, which is about one-third of our total annual consumption at the present time. .
I point out that inventories as of March 31, 1944, were 55,000,000 gallons less than at the commencement of rationing, at which time the stocks on hand were uncomfortably low.
Before I deal with aviation gasoline, I would remind hon. members that both motor and aviation gasolines come from the same sources, sources which must supply the tremendous demands of the allied armed forces. When we consider that it requires 2,000 gallons of fuel to move an armoured division one mile, that a fleet of 5,000 bombers and escort fighters raiding Germany uses up some
5.250.000	gallons of aviation gasoline, we can readily see wherein lies our responsibility.

These fighting men must not lack fuel for one single instant because of our carelessness, selfishness, or waste.
I will now give you consumption figures for aviation gasoline supplied from Canada, and these figures will indicate the importance of aviation gasoline to the Canadian war economy. Canada could not become the hub of the world's largest air training plan without sending Canadian consumption of aviation gasoline to staggering heights. By way of example, I would point out that in one thirty-day period, aircraft operated by R.C.A.F. in Canada and Newfoundland consumed an average of 548,000 gallons of aviation gasoline per day.
The figures I have for aviation gasoline, including exports from Canada, are for the five calendar years commencing with 1939 and ending with 1943, and for the twelve months ending March 31, 1944. These figures are as follows:
Gallons
1939		 5,453,980
1940		 12,661,425
1941		 57,181,005
1942		 119,740,110
1943		 173,208,910
1944	(year ended March 31)..	176,298,570
As a further indication of what the balance of this year holds in store for us, I am advised that an estimate made before the invasion indicated that we shall have to move offshore this year four times as much aviation gasoline as we did last year. What this estimate will be now, I cannot say.
I do not think it is advisable at this time to disclose aviation gasoline inventories. Meanwhile, although Canada must provide all the fuels required by its own navy

which, as hon. members know, has expanded from 13 to more than 700 vessels; although we must fuel all the bombers leaving Labrador and Newfoundland for England and leaving Edmonton for Russia; although we must fuel aircraft operating under the commonwealth air training plan, the convoys leaving our shores, the army, war factories, agricultural machinery for food production, and essential transportation, not one aircraft, ship, or machine tool has ever been stopped because of lack of fuel. We have not failed, and we must not fail.
I have pointed out to hon. members on more than one occasion that we are dependent on outside sources for 85 per cent of our petroleum product requirements, 60 per cent of which must be brought in by ocean tanker transportation which has been in short supply since 1941. We are drawing on the same sources, inventories, and transportation facilities as our allies. Coupled with this, we now face a dwindling crude oil supply. The war-

Petroleum Products
particularly now the invasion is in full swing- is making greater and greater demands upon the crude oil and transportation facilities of this hemisphere. We have to continually review our position in order to assure our allies that we are not asking for crude oil and transportation beyond our needs. Our stocks are too far below normal to carry us any distance without replenishment. Motor gasoline coupons outstanding and to be issued are based upon our inventories and projected imports which we estimate are sufficient to honour each coupon. This is not a time for other than the most essential driving. Everyone should let his conscience be his guide in using gasoline of any kind to-day-this applies to the armed forces, the farmer, and everyone else in the country.
Let me repeat: Every barrel of petroleum products we can do without means that much more for the theatres of war and the transportation to get the material there.
I will now discuss light and heavy fuel oils used for heating by Canadian homes and for heating and processing by Canadian industries. As a result of conservation measures taken on this continent, hon. members will note that whereas consumption of heavy fuel oil has dropped slightly, the consumption of light fuel oil has risen steadily since 1940. Without conservation measures our position would have been hopeless long before this, with the likelihood that many schools, office buildings, apartment houses, and homes would have been without heat last winter.
Consumption, including exports, of light fuel oils for the calendar years 1940 to 1943 and for the twelve months ending March 31, 1944, are as follows:
Gallons
1940		 201,613,895
1941		 247,578,450
1942		 251,388,585
1943		 267,139,355
1944	(year ended March 31)..	267,166,655
Light fuel oil, such as is used for heating homes, is an important commodity in the war effort, as it includes diesel oil used for propulsion of tanks and other army equipment, as well as oil for special heat treating furnaces for the annealing of metals, and for other essential uses in industry.
Heavy fuel oil consumption, including exports, for the four calendar years 1940 to 1943 inclusive, and for the twelve months ending March 31, 1944, are as follows:-
Gallons
1940		 510,191,850
1941		 590,816.485
1942		 594,590,360
1943		 560,791,910
1944	(year ended March 31)..	587,830,460
These figures do not include heavy fuel oil consumed by oil refineries.	[DOT]
At the inception of oil control we did not have in Canada an organization comparable to the American Petroleum Institute; therefore statistics kept in 1939 make no distinction between light and heavy fuel oils, but their combined consumption in that year was 589,921,360 gallons as compared with 711,805,745 gallons for 1940, 838,394,935 gallons for 1941, and 874,383,195 gallons for the year ended May 31, 1942.
Realizing that the consumption of light and heavy fuel oils might reach a point beyond our ability to supply, an appeal was made to the public in the fall of 1941 to convert to substitute fuels, and conversion for certain large groups of users was made mandatory on September 1, 1942. To what heights-the consumption of light and heavy fuel oils might have risen without restrictions I cannot say, but in reviewing the increases over the years 1939 to 1944 it is reasonable to assume that a saving of at least 175,000,000 gallons was effected. .
Light and heavy fuel oil inventories at March 31, 1944, were 4,650,065 gallons and 17,475,500 gallons respectively higher than a year ago. Because the heavier crudes we now have to run yield larger quantities of heavy fuel oil, restrictions on the use of heavy fuel oil have been lifted in all provinces except British Columbia. The situation on the west coast to-day is more critical than it has ever been since the outbreak of the war. The petroleum product requirements of the fighting forces in the Pacific are such that the oil-producing state of California is unable to meet these demands, and heavy importations are now being made from other points in the United States to California. This, of course, affects our position in British Columbia, and we are to-day moving crude oil from Colombia and Ecuador in South America to Vancouver -some 4,200 miles, or five times the distance of our previous source of supply. This has created a serious transportation problem, and it will be touch and go whether we shall be able to care for the most essential services in British Columbia.
In the winter and spring of 1942, when the supply of domestic fuel oil became acute and I announced on the floor of the house that there was evidence that this country would be short of this commodity, a number of citizens voluntarily changed over from oil to an alternative form of heating.
While no general relief can be made in respect to the use of light fuel oil for any
Petroleum Products

purpose, we have, as a result of the mild winter just behind us and the cooperation of home owners in reducing their consumption to the minimum, built up a slightly better inventory position which will permit owners of bona fide residences who voluntarily converted when requested to do so in 1942, to reinstal oil burning equipment in their homes, provided that the equipment has been continuously in their possession. This does not permit new installations.
In closing, I wish to state once again that our position in the matter of petroleum fuels is not improving, and this in spite of the best efforts we have been able to make toward conservation. Careful planning has provided gasoline available to the public in quantities sufficient to honour gasoline and fuel oil coupons which had been issued. In that respect we are more fortunate than any other country. Possibly the fact that we have kept petroleum products available for legitimate users has led to a popular belief that the supply of these products is not a critical matter. If so, the impression is erroneous and unfortunate. I am happy to say that the misuse of petroleum products has been kept to very small proportions, due wholly to the vigilance of the government's enforcement officers. I appeal for the support of the public in preventing these abuses. With the support of the public, I am hopeful that our supply position can be maintained at its present level. Without public support, I am certain that our supply position must deteriorate. Should war consumption continue at its present level for any considerable period, it is unlikely that we can avoid further curtailment in any event.

speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary assistant. I am doing so at the request of my colleague from the county of Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart), whose constituency is one of the largest producers of small fruits in Canada. According to an article appearing^ in The Country Gentleman of May, 1944, the OP.A. in the United States has eased its rules for home canning this year. They allow sugar totalling tweDty-five pounds for each member of the family, and no limitation is placed on the amount of sugar that may be used for jams, jellies and preserves. In view of this change in regulations, has the government given consideration to the advisability of increasing the ration of sugar for home canning in Canada, and, if not, will it do so immediately? This matter is urgent, because strawberries are already in full production and will be followed by raspberries, cherries and so on, in rapid succession.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT OR REESTABLISHMENT OP MEMBERS OP THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some hesitation and not a little apology for injecting some further observations on this motion for third reading, the matter having been pretty thoroughly debated. I do so, however, because the committee stage passed more quickly than I had expected, and the bill was reported while I was out of the chamber. I shall take only a few minutes to raise the one point I have in mind, which has to do with veterans of world war No. 1.
If my figures are correct, there are 11,000 of these men in the active companies of the veterans' guard alone in Canada. Then there are some 6.000 veterans of world war No. 1 in the reserve of the veterans' guard. A matter which is of concern to these men and to the public is whether or not the new Department of Veterans' Affairs will give adequate consideration to the plight of those who will be veterans of a second war and who, in view of their age, will require different treatment and a different type of rehabilitation from that used in connection with men discharged in their twenties or early thirties. I impress upon the minister the necessity of seeing to it that these men who have participated in two wars, and who have done a magnificent job in the intervening period of peace, are given special consideration in any plans and schemes the minister may have in mind. If I might add just one further sentence it would be that perhaps ex-service men in the House of Commons, in common with those throughout Canada, are a little too modest in their claims in respect of what they did in the last war, in the intervening period of peace, and during the present war. Representing a group of citizens who have been denied the privilege of service in both wars, I take this opportunity to pay tribute to those men, who have not only done their duty in time of war but have also
carried a heavy load and made a great contribution in the period of peace between the two wars.
Those who are now giving a third period of service in the present war should receive special consideration of the kind I have asked, and the treatment accorded them should be rendered willingly. I am hopeful that my remarks will not precipitate any further discussion in the matter. I rose only to say what, had I been in the house, I would have said in committee.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his suggestion,
and may say that we have already taken action along the lines suggested by him. We have a special committee dealing with demobilization, and that committee is giving special consideration to veterans of the first great war. who reenlisted in this one. My hon. friend may be sure that we will give his suggestion every consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have an opportunity to speak to this bill in the debate on second reading, and I am therefore doing so now. I believe most hon. members are agreed that the setting up of this new department, having for its purpose the concentration in one department of all affairs affecting soldiers, was overdue.
The minister was paid many compliments by various speakers respecting his management of the department of which he is now the head; and while I can agree with much of
Department of Veterans' Affairs

what was said concerning his attention to pensions affairs, yet I do not think his management of the department is altogether the measure of efficiency in the department. To my mind a proper measure of efficiency would be the number of individual cases coming before him. And if that is the measure to be applied, then I am afraid his department has not done as well as it might have. After all, if these matters were receiving in the minister's department that degree of sympathetic consideration they are supposed to receive, it would not be necessary for members in the house, veterans' organizations and other groups throughout the country to have to deal with individual cases. I believe the minister should be advised of this, and if he is to be the minister in charge of the new department he should see to it that a more sympathetic attitude is taken by certain officials in the department when they are dealing with veterans' affairs. I know that some of those officials are sympathetic, but I also know that others are not as sympathetic as they might be. Otherwise these cases would not arise in the numbers they do.
The matter about which I would speak particularly is the position, first, of old soldier settlers under the Soldier Settlement Act, and. second, of new settlers under the present Veterans' Land Act. I believe I have had as much experience with the soldier settlement board as any other member in the house, because I took up land under the act in 1919, and I believe I have made payments to the board in each of the last twenty-five years. I say therefore that I hold the viewpoint of those settlers who took land under the act. I know something about their problem, some of the reasons for failures and for success under that act. I know, too, some of the points which should be considered under the new act, if it is to be a success.
When the Soldier Settlement Act was first passed, much of the land sold to settlers was sold at inflated prices. I know of school lands held in trust by the dominion government that were put up for sale in 1918 and offered to the public at $10 an acre. A soldier returned within six months after that sale vyas held and offered the school lands board $10 an acre. He was told that he could not. buy the land at that price. Within three months he was notified by the soldier settlement board that under the new act the land was now available, through that board, and they quoted a price to him of $21 per acre on land which had been offered to the general public for $10 an acre less than a year before. The land was bought at $21 an acre under the soldier settlement board. Another quarter oh the same section which was held at $23

an. acre later reverted to the school lands department and was again offered for sale and bought by the same soldier settler at $15 an acre in 1927. The inflated value placed on lands at that time constituted one of the chief reasons why the soldiers under the old soldier settlement board act were unable to meet their commitments.
This may be past history; there are those who may say that that is not happening now. But it is happening; it is happening to-day. Some of this very land which was taken back by the soldier settlement board in the thirties and was being offered to the general public in 1939 is being held at twenty to thirty per cent over pre-war prices for sale to men coming back and taking up land under the new legislation. That is a wrong example for the government to set. Why land values should be increased to new settlers to-day I do not know. I say it is wrong. The original grant provided by the government for buying land and buildings was $3,600, but it was found necessary to increase it to $4,800 in order that suitable holdings might be secured. That extra $1,200 represents debt as far as the new veteran is concerned; it also represents dollars in the pockets of the land companies. Why the boys who are fighting overseas should be expected to meet this additional charge for the benefit of land companies is something I do not understand. The government should take the matter into consideration. These lands should have been taken over at their 1939 prices and held at those figures for the boys coming back from overseas; no inflated values should have been permitted on account of increased prices during the war.
The same consideration applies to stock and implements. Present prices of stock and equipment are much higher than they were in 1939, but there is no guarantee that high prices will continue during the years in which these settlers are going to be paying for their land. That is one of the reasons why I suggested in the committee that a parity clause should be inserted in the new veterans' land act whereby the year in which the land was bought should be taken as the basis, and any decrease or increase in the value of produce sold should be taken into consideration in fixing the payments to be made in the years to come. If such a clause had been written into the old soldier settlement board act, many of the difficulties which arose under that act would not have occurred.
When land was purchased under that measure in 1919 and 1920 in western Canada, wheat was over $2 a bushel, and other grains, as well as stock and equipment, were selling at proportionately high prices. There was also
JUiNE 20, 1944
Department of Veterans' Affairs
laxity in the matter of proper investigation as to suitability of the land and stock which were purchased. When I was working for a farmer in western Canada in 1919 I saw a soldier settlement board inspector purchasing for a soldier settler milch cow's which were supposed to be fresh cows but were far from being that, and the prices paid were out of line with those which should have been paid. I do not know whether, it was ignorance on the part of the inspector or whether it was collusion, but undoubtedly a great deal of stock was bought at that time at unreasonably high prices. The same thing is likely to occur again unless more care is taken than was shown twenty-five years ago; and judging by the way purchases are now being made I am doubtful whether that extra care is being taken.
It is because of such circumstances as I have outlined that old soldier settlers find themselves in their present position. That is why, some three or four weeks ago, a delegation came here to ask that these men be given clear titles to their land before the new statute comes into force. The delegation appeared before the government, or a committee of the government, who listened to their representation and said that consideration will be given to it. What consideration is being or will be given remains to be seen. But certainly those men are entitled to consideration.
In speaking to some of the departmental officials I have heard them express the opinion that if there are yet a number of settlers who have not met their commitments, it is because of lack of will on their part to do so. From personal knowledge of many of these men I say that that is not a fact. Many of them experienced sickness in their families; they had to choose between having sufficient money to provide their wives or children with medical attention, and meeting their payments to the board; and I think they were entitled to put the medical care of their families ahead of their obligations under their contracts. In many of the cases they fell into arrears because they wished to give their children a proper education. I know a number of soldiers of the last war who have families of four, five or six children and had to choose between educating them and meeting their payments to the soldier settlement board. They were making a far greater contribution to the welfare of Canada by educating their families than they would have done by meeting their payments in full to the board, because to-day many of their children are overseas fighting in our forces and able to do so more efficiently as a result of the education which they received.
These are some of the reasons why these settlers find themselves in the position they are in to-day, and I urge that the government give sympathetic consideration to their request to have title granted to their land.
Another point which I commend to the attention of the minister is the writing of a parity clause into contracts under the new Veterans' Land Act. I believe it is one of the elements most essential to the success of this measure. It does not matter much what the contract is to-day; the real question is what relation it will have to the prices of products five or ten years from now when payments have to be made. This will be the deciding factor as to whether the settler can meet his obligations. If he is purchasing land to-day at values related to the present prices of grain, live stock and dairy products, those prices should be taken into account when he is paying for his land. Unless that is done I cannot see how the settler under the new act will be in a much better position than were the settlers under the old act.
I also wish to emphasize the insufficiency of the amount now made available for procuring stock and equipment under the new measure. Our boys are overseas fighting to-day. We place in their hands a bomber costing a quarter of a million dollars or a tank to the value of $50,000 for the purpose of winning the war, but when they come home we give them $1,200 to buy stock and equipment to reestablish themselves. Any farmer knows how far $1,200 will go to-day in buying stock and equipment. It is just about sufficient for two old horses and some second-hand machinery. If that is the best we can do, after we have placed in the hands of our boys at the front equipment worth tens of thousands of dollars, it is time we had another think coming. I do not believe the boys will accept this. I am sure it is not good enough. I certainly think that the amount of money made available for stock and equipment should be increased.
With respect to the amount of money made available for full-time farming purposes, $4,800 to-day just does not buy an economic farming unit either in eastern or in western Canada. Anyone who is engaged in farming knows that in western Canada the economic farming unit must be at least one section of land, or, better still, one and a half or two sections. The sum of $4,800 will buy a quarter-section, and even if the man gets it free he still has not enough land on which to make a living at farming, educate his family and pay for proper health services. I would say that $10,000 is much nearer the sum required to purchase an economic unit for full-time farming anywhere
Department oj Reconstruction

in Canada, and I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to raising the amount of money that will be made available to these men for the purchase of a full-time farming unit. It is better to lend a man $10,000 to buy a farm that he has a chance to pay for than to lend him $4,800 for a farm on which you know and I know, Mr. Speaker, he cannot meet the payments. The larger unit is the economic unit, with the farm equipped with modern machinery.
These are just a few of the matters I wished to bring to the minister's attention with respect to the soldier settler and the Veterans' Land Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of bill No. 82 to establish a Department of Reconstruction.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that the speech from the throne made mention of three new departments, each of which has to do with some phase of reconstruction in the broad sense of that word. One is the Department of Veterans' Affairs, which is concerned particularly with matters relating to demobilization and rehabilitation of the armed forces. Another is the Department of Social Welfare, the designation of which, by the way, I am going to ask the house to allow me to amend and have it named the Department of National Health and Welfare. I might say that the wording "Social Welfare" was selected because of the comprehensive nature of the term. It was thought that welfare included health. But there have been representations to the government, which I think have been sound, that we have had a department of health in Canada for some time past, the Department of National Health, and that to eliminate that particular designation might cause it to be assumed that the government was paying less attention rather than more attention to the question of national health. I imagine that there will be no objection to the acceptance of the amended designation of that department.
The third department mentioned is the Department of Reconstruction. The first two departments I have referred to grow, in a way, out of the existing Department of Pensions and National Health. The Department of Reconstruction is an entirely new department

of government and will be concerned with aspects of government business for which hitherto no one minister has been responsible.
In considering the Department of Reconstruction, it is necessary in the first instance to understand clearly what is meant by reconstruction. There are different interpretations given to the term. Reconstruction in the war zones where there has been a wholesale destruction of property and community life will mean the physical rebuilding of the areas that have been devastated. Fortunately in Canada we have not suffered from anything of the kind. We have not had our homes bombed; we have not had our railways and roads destroyed; we have not had our industries reduced-rather, if anything, we have had our industries vastly increased and extended as the result of the war effort of the country. We are fortunate, I say, in that particular. Reconstruction with us, and, indeed, reconstruction everywhere in the broad sense of the word, means the transforming of a nation that has been carrying on war and has been geared for war and has a war economy, back to a nation that is returning to its peaceful pursuits; to the ordinary life which the community and the nation carry on in time of peace. That broad conception of reconstruction necessarily includes much in the way of the physical rebuilding and development of the country, but it includes also matters which relate to social security, questions of health and social welfare. Of course, above all else, it includes the rehabilitation of members of the armed forces and the finding of new employment in peaceful vocations for those now engaged in war industries.
There is one aspect of reconstruction which might be termed economic reconstruction. That has to do largely with the transforming of industry from making war supplies to making goods for human consumption and with restoring and increasing the capital equipment of the nation, together with the provision of employment for those who are being transferred from the one activity to the other. It is in connection with this economic reconstruction that the new Department of Reconstruction of the federal government will be primarily concerned.
On April 17 last I introduced the resolution on which this bill is based and spoke at some length upon aspects of the proposed bill. I do not wish to repeat to-day what was said then, except in one or two particulars. I indicated clearly the need for a department concerned with the work of physical reconstruction. I should like to quote the words which I then used, which will be found on page 2085 of Hansard:

Department oj Reconstruction
The problem of reconstruction will involve the reemployment of nearly two million Canadians now in the armed forces, the merchant navy or war industry. Employment must be productive and must contribute to a rising standard of living. The great industrial plant created for war purposes must be transformed to meet peace time demands in Canada or abroad. Markets must be found and retained for our greatly increased food production unless we are not to face an agricultural depression. Railways, highways and other capital equipment which has suffered the strain of war must be reconstituted. Civilian aviation and other new means of transport and communication must be developed. Public works and conservation and development projects _ will be required, particularly while private industries are being converted to peace time operations. New housing, both urban and rural, improvements to existing housing and community planning can contribute at once to the volume of employment and the improvement of the standard of living.	_
These are merely a few of the directions in which reconstruction planning requires to be carried on. Obviously most, if not all, of these functions relate specifically to some existing department of government.
I wish first to make it perfectly clear that in establishing the Department of Reconstruction the government is not establishing a department which will be primarily an administrative department to carry on under its own immediate officials the work of -econstruction.
The work of reconstruction will necessarily be carried on in largest part, in fact almost entirely, by existing departments of government, and not merely by departments of the federal government, but by departments of provincial governments and municipalities as well. Indeeed, in changing our national economy from a war-time to a peace-time basis, almost every department of government will have some special work to do.
First and foremost there is the obligation to ensure the establishment of what may be most effective in the way of world organization for peace. That in itself is an exceedingly large task. It will involve consideration primarily by the Department of External Affairs, in so far as one department rather than another in Canada may be concerned. It is a task in which bodies, such as the League of Nations Society and the like, will be interested, a great work requiring the assistance of several agencies of government. Probably more than any other single question requiring attention in the post-war period will be the securing of wider markets and the extension of trade.
One hears th- question asked very often to-day, Why is it that we are able to do in time of war, and to do so effectively, many of the things which it seems impossible for us to do in time of peace? I should like to answer that question at once from the two points of view. The first is that in time of war, happily,
all the united nations have the same purpose and are prepared to work together toward the furthering of a particular end. There has been little difficulty, since this war began, in effecting among the united nations the most complete kind of cooperation toward a particular end. In time of peace, unfortunately, cooperation among nations has been very far from the rule. Instead of nations seeking to work together, for example, toward the expansion of trade generally throughout the world, many nations have taken the view that the way in which more employment can be obtained1 is for one country to prevent some other country from having its people employed to the extent that they should be. If, as a group of nations interested in having world peace, we of the united nations can help develop trade throughout all parts of the world we shall perhaps be taking the most effective of all steps in the direction of bringing about those conditions which, for Canada particularly, it will be necessary to establish if we are to have the development of our great primary industries carried to the extent that they should be. What we can do in the way of agriculture, the mining, fishing and forestry industries in this country will depend on the markets we are able to obtain, and the markets we are able to obtain will depend on the extent to which the nations of the world come to a correct point of view as to what it is that makes most for the prosperity of all.
We shall do well, I believe, to bear in mind that prosperity is indivisible. It is not something which one nation can have and enjoy by itself; it is something that has to be shared. We shall have to come to see that we are members one of another and that no nation livet.h unto itself. As we achieve this larger conception we shall be furthering the fundamental condition required to ensure the fullest employment for the great mass of the men and women in this country.
The second reason, why we have been more successful in time of war in doing some of the things we are unable to effect in peace, is that, under the War Measures Act, the government has constitutional authority to see that its policies are carried out. It is in a position to act for the whole of Canada in regard to the prosecution of the war. In times of peace, on the other hand, we have to strive, in carrying out any policy, to get the good will and effective cooperation of every province, as well as carrying out our own work. I hope and believe, as a result of what has happened during the past five years, and of the cooperation which the federal government has had in large measure

speechtext:
from the provincial governments, that following conferences still to be held between the provinces and ourselves we shall be able to work out some means whereby we can, in the period after the war, secure still greater cooperation for the benefit of all.
These two considerations, I believe, will serve to answer the particular question as to why it is that we do effectively in time of war many of the things which we seem unable to do in times of peace. But in connection with any policy of reconstruction there will be matters that relate not only to trade but also to the development of industry and transportation, the development of aviation, of merchant shipping, of irrigation, the development of all our natural resources, housing and community planning, and also many other matters which have been discussed in this house during this session. At the moment I wish to emphasize that reconstruction is not concerned merely with public works and the carrying out of new undertakings of the kind. They will of necessity constitute one phase of the work of reconstruction, and there will be great need for new developments as well as to make up for what has been postponed in that way during the past few years. But reconstruction, in the broad sense of the term, will involve, as I say, not merely what one department of government is in a position to carry out but to a considerable extent what all departments of government can do in a variety of fields.
What is true of the federal government departments is equally true of the governments of the provinces. Fortunately, in the different provinces, some provision has already been made for the work of planning and development. That work in some respects parallels what is or will be carried out in the federal field. It will be necessary, if both federal and provincial policies are to be carried on without waste and overlapping, and if gaps are to be avoided here and there, which may affect the national structure, that some central agency should have, the duty of seeing that coordination is effected in the best manner possible. That cannot be done by leaving it without special responsibility to the ministers of the different departments, each of whom is concerned with a particular work. Moreover, what is the concern of all is very often apt to be the least concern of any. It is desirable, therefore, that there should be in the administration at this time, as the country begins to look forward to reverting to an economy for peace, some one minister who will have constantly before him the duty of seeing that what is necessaiy in

the formulation and the carrying out of policies of reconstruction, is effectively undertaken.
The purpose of this bill, which is now before the house for second reading is, as stated in tihe explanatory note:
. . . to establish a department of reconstruction under the direction of a minister of reconstruction who shall be responsible for preparing and coordinating plans and projects for reconstruction, and making provision for carrying out such plans with the authorization of the governor in council.
Personally I should have preferred to see that explanatory note worded somewhat differently to bring out the full intent and purpose of its provisions. I should like to have it read:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a department of reconstruction under the direction of a minister of reconstruction who shall be responsible for seeing that reconstruction plans and projects are prepared or formulated and coordinated, and that provision shall be made for carrying out such plans with the authorization of the governor in council.
As the explanatory note reads, it might be assumed that the minister himself had to make all the plans and administer them. That is not the intention. It will be the minister's duty to see that plans are made. It will also be his duty to see that plans having to do with reconstruction are carried out. But these duties will be carried on in cooperation with his colleagues of other government departments.
In this particular, the present bill follows the example that has been set by the government of the United Kingdom where one minister of the crown has been appointed minister of reconstruction. As hon. members know, some seven months ago Lord Woollton was appointed Minister of Reconstruction in the United Kingdom. When he addressed the House of Lords and described his functions he began by saying that he had no office or permanent staff; that it was his intention to perform the major part of his duties by thinking over the many problems that had to be worked out and presenting suggestions to his colleagues, discussing them in cabinet council with the committee which would be there for the purpose of assisting him in that work. Lord Woollton has carried on very largely in that way. He heads no department of government; he is not the head of a ministry. He is simply the Minister of Reconstruction. He has associated with him experts on different aspects of reconstruction. He consults with them and with a committee of the war cabinet, of which he himself is a member. Plans are then presented to and discussed by the war cabinet or the cabinet as a whole, and work to be carried out is assigned to the appropriate departments of the government.
JtJNE 20, 1944
Department oj Reconstruction
It is the intention under this bill to appoint as Minister of Reconstruction in Canada one of the ministers' of the crown who holds office at the present time, and who heads one of the departments of government. He will continue to administer the department of which he is now the head, but he will also have the special duty of meeting with experts on reconstruction, of meeting with a committee of the cabinet which will be composed of ministers who will also be expected to give their time and thought to the formulating of plans related to reconstruction, and to seeing that these plans are carried out. As part of his duty there will be also the obligation of keeping himself informed with respect to what has been and is being done by the provinces and municipalities, and, as far as it may be possible through consultation with them, and in other ways, of seeking to combine in the most effective way the work of reconstruction of the federal government and of the provincial governments and municipalities.
The difference in scope and in procedure in the present bill from the British procedure where it exists arises out of the difference in our own country from Britain in the matter of jurisdiction with respect to legislative powers. In Britain the central government has charge of pretty nearly everything, except . what the municipalities may be charged with. As an example let me make mention of education. As all hon. members know, education in Canada is one of the subjects specially assigned to the provincial governments. I shall not enumerate the different duties of the federal and provincial governments, or what is reserved to one or to the other. As we know, there are instances where, both dominion and provincial governments have jurisdiction, for example, in matters relating to agriculture, public works, and immigration. In all of these fields there is jurisdiction in which both the provincial and federal governments share.
In the reconstructing of the nation from a war-time to a peace-time economy, it is important that departments which are doing similar work should work together in harmony as largely as possible, not only as between the dominion and one province but as between the dominion and all the provinces, and between the provinces themselves. Obviously no minister of the crown could by himself be expected to take that work of coordination completely in hand. He would have to have associated with him not only experts but a considerable staff. He would have to have a deputy minister who is in a position to communicate authoritatively with the governments of the provinces, with municipalities,
with business organizations, professional organizations, private industries and individuals. For that reason the present bill contemplates the establishment of a department with a deputy minister and with such staff as may be essential for the carrying on of that class of work-not a large staff, because it is not contemplated that this department is going to last for all time. The department is being set up at this time for a special purpose related to special conditions, just as certain departments of the federal government were set up at the beginning of the war to do war work. For example, the Department of Munitions and Supply was set up to carry on an important phase of war work. When the war ends that department will fade out; but, with the preparation for peace and for developing the national economy to further the pursuits of peace, it will be necessary to have some one department that will be specially charged with that all-important work. The Department of Reconstruction will have that particular duty.
I do not think I need to enlarge upon the duties of the minister or the staff. Questions may be answered in detail in committee. I should however like to say a word immediately with respect to the comment that one sometimes hears to the effect that the government is late, in setting up this department. Well, I take complete issue with that criticism. First of all, may I say that in its main task, to do what is possible to ensure full employment in the country, the need for this department is not likely to be felt to any considerable extent for some time to come. During the war, as we all know, full employment has developed in the industries essential for carrying on the war. But the war is not over yet. We do not know how long the war in Europe is going to last, and when the war is over in Europe no one will venture to say how long the war' against Japan may continue. Certainly this country will continue to do its full share towards an all-out war effort until the war is won both in the orient and in Europe. There is likely to be a very large demand for war materials as long as that period continues; but once the war is over there will be a new kind of demand for materials and services and supplies, which will be very great. That demand will arise in the transitional period from war to peace in the countries of Europe, as well as in our own, and in all countries that have been affected by the war.
The relief and rehabilitation of the peoples of Europe are certainly likely to create a demand for commodities of different kinds which it will be difficult to meet. We all remember what took place at the end of the last war.

251J
Department oj Reconstruction

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The end of the last war was followed by a boom. There has not been on this continent at any time the same sudden increase of demand for supplies, services and labour, as there was in the years immediately following 1918, the years 1919 and 1920. In other words, a boom situation was created, but it was followed by an appalling depression. That is one of the things that we must certainly seek to avoid in dealing with the post-war period. We have the experience of that time before us, and, fortunately, we have the benefit of the careful research that has been carried on in all parts of the world as to its causes, so that to-day we have the knowledge of the action needed to prevent the recurrence of that sort of thing. There again, if this kind of disaster is to be prevented, it seems to me desirable that there should be some member of the government who will have a special responsibility to see that measures to avoid periods of depression and unemployment are carefully thought out, studied in advance and, as far as possible, given effect. The Minister of Reconstruction will have as part of his obligation to see that in planning a long-range view as well as a short range view is taken. Of necessity, immediately the war ends and people begin to be transferred from one employment to another, some men and women will be out of employment for a short time. There will continue to be occupational causes which will tend to throw men out of work at certain seasons of the year. Unemployment of that kind will necessarily occur. But broadly speaking, looking at mass employment as it presents itself over a period of months and years, the period immediately following the close of the war should be a time in which there will be a large demand for labour. The danger will come after that, and the only way it can be met is by careful planning now and in the period of transition, by seeking to effect that kind of cooperation between the provinces and the dominion in our own country, and between our country and other countries, which will help prevent a period of depression.
Another reason why, up to the moment, it has not seemed essential to have a department particularly concerned with reconstruction, a reason perhaps the stronger of the two in its immediate application is that almost since the very beginning of the war a careful study has been carried on by the government, followed later by committees of this parliament, by provincial governments, municipalities, societies, organizations, business and private interests, of matters pertaining to reconstruction in all its phases. I might give the house, in quick succession, the names of
{Mr. Mackenzie King.}
some of these committees and make mention of some of the things which already have been done. The war had scarcely begun before the present administration realized that the demobilization and rehabilitation of the men serving overseas would inevitably be an important question that could not receive attention too soon, and a committee of the cabinet to consider this problem was formed before the end of 1939. We in Canada had a committee on the subject of demobilization and rehabilitation before the British government appointed any such committee. Hon. members will recall that Mr. Chamberlain was Prime Minister of Great Britain at the beginning of the war. He was succeeded by Mr. Churchill, and it was not until after Mr. Churchill had been in office for a short time that the British government appointed a committee of the cabinet to study these problems and to prepare policies which would help meet them. On December 9 the cabinet in Canada appointed a committee on demobilization and reestablishment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: In what year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
On December 9, 1939, a government committee on demobilization and reestablishment was set up. Members of this committee soon realized that demobilization and rehabilitation was only one of the great aspects of the problem of reconstruction. Subsequently the scope of the committee was enlarged, under an order in council dated February 17, 1941, to include all phases of reconstruction, and at the same time an advisory committee on reconstruction was set up on an informal basis. As hon. members will recall, this advisory committee was headed by Principal James of McGill university. The government was anxious to have associated with it, altogether outside the administration, advisers who would go carefully into the problems of reconstruction. On September 2, 1941, this committee was given formal character by order in council. I need not take time at the moment to speak of the work of the James committee, though up to the present far too little reference I think has been made to it. As hon. members are aware, the committee has published a number of valuable reports. The main report, on reconstruction, was published on September 24, 1943. Then there was a special report on the conservation and development of natural resources; a report on publicly-financed construction projects; a report on post-war employment; a report on the post-war problems of women, and a report on housing. These matters have been studied as well by officials of departments of the government during the past year or two, and

Department of Reconstruction
the government has had the benefit of their reports and reports of the James committee to guide it in its work.
In addition the government recognized at an early stage the service that might be rendered by members of both houses of this parliament in the study of these questions and in a considering of recommendations which might come from any source in any part of Canada. On March 24, 1942, this house established a committee on reconstruction and reestablishment. That committee was reappointed in 1943 and again this year. In 1943 a senate committee on economic reestablishment and social security was appointed. I should like to pause for a moment to thank hon. members of these committees for the assistance they have given and to say, on behalf of the government, how deepfy indebted we feel particularly to the special committee on reconstruction of this house, of which the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon) was chairman. That committee was composed of members from all sides of the house. It is generally acknowledged that the chairman discharged his duties to the entire satisfaction of the committee, and that the committee's work has been not only comprehensive but constructively helpful in the fullest meaning of that term. The fact that the house has not discussed at length the various matters referred to in these reports does not mean that the reports themselves have not been useful and of great service to the government. As a matter of fact they have been of the greatest help; they have served as guides to the ministers in charge of the different departments in taking up some of the subjects, and have been helpful to the government in planning its programme. Indeed, one of the recommendations made by the committee of this House of Commons had to do with the establishment of the very department of which I am speaking at the moment. That recommendation was made a year or so ago. The new department has not been set up until the present for reasons I have given already.
I have mentioned only some of the reports that have been made to the federal government by various bodies connected with it. There has been an advisory committee on economic policy appointed on January 23, 1943, composed of senior officials, under the chairmanship of Mr. W. C. Clark. This committee has since been continuously investigating and studying the post-war problems. At that time the James committee became directly responsible to the President of the Privy Council. It presented its final report on September 24, 1943, at which time the advisory committee on economic policy took over its work.
Since the James committee completed its work the advisory committee on economic policy has also taken over the work formerly carried on by the James committee.
If it were needed to specify the extent to which the reports have served as a basis for legislation, I could refer to many matters which have been discussed in the house already, conspicuous among the number being the bill which received third reading only this afternoon, namely the bill establishing a department of veterans' affairs. There has been a full discussion on that measure during the last few days. There could be no better evidence that the government has not been neglecting the question of reconstruction than the measures already enacted pertaining to war veterans' affairs. We began with the most important of all, namely, those matters which pertain to the demobilization and rehabilitation of the armed forces. I think the house must now be convinced that not only was a very comprehensive programme outlined, but that already in the main it has been enacted and is now in force.
What is true of the Department of Veterans' Affairs, and the work concerning war veterans, is true to no lesser extent of some of the other work of the government pertaining to reconstruction. I might refer, for example, to matters pertaining to the expansion of trade which have been a special concern of the departments of external affairs, trade and commerce and finance. Many of our war policies have been and will prove to be of the greatest possible assistance in connection with the post-war effort. In fact, in shaping all our war policies we have had the post-war situation very much in mind.
Let me deal with some of these policies. We have been seeking not to build up intergovernmental debts between nations. It will be recalled this was the first obstacle that confronted the nations once the last war was over. Our aim there, in concert with other nations, has been to prevent an accumulation and combination of obligations. The system of Mutual Aid has for its object the avoidance of unwieldy debts between governments, as well as helping to effect an all-out war effort, and give maximum employment to our own people. Exchange control and price control policies will also help in trading relations of the future. The work in connection with UNRRA, which has to do with relief and rehabilitation in the devastated areas and starving populations of Europe, is a great work which has been established in this period of war, but all of which relates to the post-war period. It will have much to do with maintaining a high
Department of Reconstruction

level of employment in Canada for some [DOT] time to come. All of this will have to do with increasing our production-production in agriculture, mines, fisheries and forests. On the orderly resumption of external trade and its expansion, the prosperity of agriculture, the forest industries, mining, fishing and many of our manufacturing industries depend. So that it is folly for'anyone to say that, up to the present time, little or nothing has been done by way of reconstruction, just because one particular department bearing that name, and having the purposes in view I have mentioned, has not been established until now. The establishment of the department is only the latest of a long list of measures designed to further the work of reconstruction.
There have been discussions on monetary matters. We have not waited until the war was over to have those matters explored; they *are being explored at the present time. I cannot say how successful they may be. At any rate, wherever in the past experience has shown failure, we have tried to anticipate a similar situation and to meet it before it occurs again. The government will assist wherever it can in the development of international arrangements concerning currency and trade, the government intends to join in a progressive freeing of world trade from the whole network of quotas, payment agreements and other similar restrictions and a progressive reduction of tariffs.
Several measures have been introduced at .this session, or are about to be introduced, which relate to reconstruction in the post-war 'period. They are based in large part upon studies which have been carefully carried out either by government officials or by committees of the house, or have come to the government from other sources. For example, there is a measure to guarantee or ensure export credits, to which reference was made in the speech from the throne. That measure will be introduced shortly. Then there is provision for the expansion of the trade commissioner service, which was also forecast in the speech from the throne.
Hon. members *will recall that the house is discussing in some detail matters respecting civil aviation and aeronautics. These are measures which relate to the post-war rather than to the war period. For two years past an interdepartmental committee has been at work on civil aviation. The government's policy-a complete plan-was outlined to the house a year ago. A draft international agreement has been put forward by Canada. There is an interdepartmental committee on merchant shipping actively at work considering post-war shipping policies which will be required.

In connection with the work of industrial conversion, hon. members will recall that in November of last year a crown assets allocation committee and War Assets Corporation Ltd. was set up by order in council. Only the night before last, a bill respecting the disposition of surplus crown assets passed the house. That bill dealt with obsolete and unused war materials.
An industrial development bank bill was introduced in February of this year and has since been passed. There has been a constant study by different departments and agencies of government of the general problems of reconversion of industry. These matters have been considered specially by the Department of Munitions and Supply, the wartime prices and trade board and the advisory committee on economic policy. Later, as forecast in the speech from the throne, there will be some tax modifications to encourage industrial conversion, and also there will be an expansion of research.
Only this afternoon an hon. member referred to the government's promise to appoint a fuel commission, to consider problems of the coal industry. That commission has not yet been established; but it- will be. Its work will have relation to matters pertaining to the post-war period in that great industry.
I might mention another very important measure already passed, namely the Unemployment Insurance Act. Hon. members may forget that measure was enacted since the war began. It was passed by this parliament in July, 1940. We were not waiting until the war was over to take steps to prepare for possible conditions of post-war unemployment.
Similarly, we have taken action with respect to an employment service, and hon. members know that national selective service has been developed. It will have to work in reverse when we reach the close of hostilities and the return to the pursuits of peace. Much has been done by way of war-time vocational training, which is providing experience and organization for post-war technical training.
The promise was made in the speech from the throne-and it will be implemented, as all the other measures so promised are being implemented-for a floor under farm prices after the war. Again, the government is not waiting until the war is over to make provision for the post-war. Provision is being made for agricultural credits, through the Bank Act as revised, and a farm improvement credit bill which has been introduced-
Similarly, provision for credit to fishermen is being made in the Bank Act, and special study is being given to the post-war problems of the fishing industry.

Department oj Reconstruction
I should also mention one of the most important pieces of legislation namely that respecting housing. As yet, that legislation has not been brought in, but lion, members are aware that for the last two years the govern meat has been giving special consideration to the housing problem, and has been carrying on active work in that connection. On may 11, a preview was given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) of some features of housing legislation. Recently a national adviser on community planning was appointed by the Minister of Finance.
I could speak further about the public works development and the valuable recommendations of the House of Commons committees in the past two sessions and of the James committee which are being or will be implemented. As I already said, the new Department of Reconstruction will have the duty of formulating policies and coordinating activities of various federal departments and agencies; also the vital task of working out cooperation with the provinces which, because they control natural resources, are largely concerned with this field.
By a further step, we hope to ensure more effective cooperation between the provinces and ourselves through holding, before long we hope, a dominion-provincial conference, to take up some of the questions which must be squarely faced, if conditions in the postwar period are to be adequately met.

I will put it this way to my hon. friend. In this period of war we have been able to raise money through loans and taxation, for what purpose? For the purpose mainly of spending the money on destruction, on the destruction of property, the destruction of community and national life, and human lives; all of which indicates that instead of having our taxes serve a useful constructive purpose, they are serving, of necessity-it is not our fault, it is part of the penalty of war-the needs of destruction. When the whole picture is reversed, and it comes to be a matter of carrying out constructive work, work for the rebuilding of communities, for the supplying of homes, and the needs of homes, the necessaries and conveniences of life, many of which have been absolutely prohibited in the period of war, there is going to be a demand for employment the like of which has not arisen at any other time, and as one want is satisfied another want is sure to be created. My hon. friend remembers, I suppose, the little fable of the man who cut away at a tree and every time he took one chip out two appeared in its place. That mythical tale has always seemed a bit of a mystery to me, but I think I realize what was meant. I think it applies to human need -or human greed, if you wish it. The minute you satisfy one need or want you create two more.
I will illustrate. The moment a man is fortunate enough to get a house he immediately wants to have the house properly furnished.
