speechtext:
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) read over the explanatory note he suggested that it would have been better if it had had a few extra words. With that I agree. If I remember, the Prime Minister said that after the word "plans" something like the following should be added, "are prepared and coordinated and must be carried out." I believe that if that suggestion of the Prime Minister is acted upon by the coming minister of reconstruction, something worthwhile will be done.
Before proceeding with what I propose to say I should like to make a short reference to the parliamentary reconstruction committee. I have not sat on any previous committee of which the members, irrespective of party, were as nearly unanimous in suggesting a plan and a programme and more ready to listen to plans and programmes than were the members of this committee. There was no conflict between them. The witnesses who came before the committee were as a whole earnest, capable men and women of high calibre, and some of our advisers may fairly be described as brilliant. I ought to say, too, that we had an excellent chairman. I might say more if he were not sitting in this chamber. He was an indefatigable worker; he must have been sitting up all hours of the night making plans and preparations to invite before the committee those whom the steering committee and himself thought would be best capable of making helpful proposals.

Department oj Reconstruction
I am glad that the government has accepted the recommendation of the committee and is now setting up a department of reconstruction.
I believe that the first report of the committee that asked for the setting up of such a department was tabled in this house on June 23, 1943. The committee's recommendation read:
In view of all the foregoing, your committee recommends that the Canadian government give immediate consideration to your committee's strong opinion that the government should take the necessary steps either by the establishment of some body, to be organized under ministerial responsibility, or otherwise to provide for the carrying out of works such as those contemplated in the preceding portions of this report.
Then in its fourth report tabled on January 26 the committee through its chairman presented similar recommendations. I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support the motion for the second reading of the bill which has just been introduced by the Prime Minister to establish a department of reconstruction.
Six provinces in all appeared before the committee. The three other provinces have since, I believe, set up their own reconstruction committees. Each one of the provinces that appeared before the committee advanced very constructive proposals for after-the-war rehabilitation of returned soldiers and of those employed in industry. Perhaps I should say a word about the proposals of one or two of the provinces that appeared before the committee.
I did not happen to be present when the maritime provinces appeared before the committee; I had to be away on that occasion. The province of Saskatchewan appeared before the committee and made very constructive suggestions, the carrying out of which would mean a great deal to the province itself and would provide much employment. There is no reason why such a large programme should not be carried out. The Saskatchewan programme covered such matters as public works, universities, schools, roads, the improvement of the telephone system, reforestation, a fire prevention programme, parks, mapping and so forth. The whole programme was estimated to cost between $175,000,000 and $200,000,000. The carrying out of a programme of that magnitude could not, of course, be done within a year or two. I have forgotten the length of their programme but I believe it was to take five years or more. I hope that when the representatives of the Saskatchewan government come down here after the war to ask for assistance in carrying out the programme which the recent government of that province submitted they will receive support from this parliament.
The same thing might be said of the Alberta proposals. I shall give just one example of after-the-war rehabilitation proposals that were submitted by the Alberta government, because I do not want to go into too much detail. The Alberta government did submit a programme of which I personally am strongly in favour, namely an irrigation programme. They set out the programme in detail for irrigating one million acres not now irrigated. Anyone who has travelled through southern Alberta and has seen, as I have seen, the tremendous results that accrue from a policy of irrigation-it is a self-liquidating project, paying for its cost by the returns-could not but support the irrigation programme submitted by the Alberta government. They pointed out that their programme would mean
9.500	new farms receiving water from the irrigation canals, farms which would produce crops such as are now produced on irrigated land in southern Alberta. If that programme were carried out it would mean an increase in population of some 50,000 people in the province. Think for a moment of the increase there would be in employment from the opening up of 9,500 new sure-crop farms. It would mean 9,500 new homes, with all that pertains to the construction of a home and all that is installed within a home, and all the equipment necessary to operate a farm. As was proven by the Alberta submission, and as those who study irrigation know, irrigation projects liquidate themselves by the returns that come from each irrigated acre. The programme of the Alberta government is one that to my mind would provide not only large employment in Alberta but also very considerable employment in factories down here in Ontario, in Quebec and in the maritime provinces. One cannot conceive of an increase of 50,000 in population and the construction of
9.500	new homes and the opening up of that many new farms without realizing the tremendous ramifications of employment that would result from such a programme, extending not only to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia as well as Alberta but all across Canada.
These are two examples of the programmes submitted by different provinces that appeared before the committee. Each province had its own problems and programmes, and perhaps before I sit down I shall perhaps make a recapitulation of some of them. I have no doubt whatever that, whoever the new minister of this department may be, he will be seized of the importance of expanding the irrigation systems in Alberta and creating new ones and making available the necessary water as a means of providing a vast amount of
Department of Reconstruction

surveying but of compiling their statistics. I cannot believe that there will be any unemployment after the war if we use our heads, if we all work together and make certain that in this country, a land flowing with milk and honey and with incomparable resources, the like of which no other country in the world has, with opportunities to produce power and everything else that is required, opportunities are afforded to take advantage of our resources, there would be no unemployment in Canada.
We had representatives of labour come before us. We found them very satisfactory and in earnest that there should be no unemployment after the war. If labour cooperates with everybody else, as honest labour always does, they will help materially. Labour has many good sane leaders. I do not know any who are not in that class. With good sane leadership labour can and will assist in seeing to it that there will be no unemployment in this country after the war. We also had representatives from the department of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). I was about to say that those representatives dealt with not a big matter, but one that is filled with a good deal of hope. They came before us to explain the building up of the fur industry which the minister himself has been initiating during the last two or three years. That will result in a lot of employment among certain classes of people who do not get much employment. I was greatly pleased with what the representatives of the department told the committee with respect to the proposed fur production programme of the Department of Mines and Resources and how it would result in giving employment. I cannot touch on many items; I mention them as they come to my mind. The one I have just mentioned is only one of many such programmes that were submitted to the committee.
We had the coal men before us. I may say that the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) was a great help to us in elucidating the programme presented by the coal people. With a national coal programme in Canada after the war there is no reason why we should not be able to give thousands upon thousands more of coal men work in the coal mines of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta, British Columbia and wherever else there are mines. If we would only use our heads, Your Honour, there would not need to be any unemployment in this country. If we all work together, thinking only of Canada, we would prevent an unemployment problem in Canada after the war.
I should like to refer to one gentleman who came before the committee, a humble, capable 
man	from Alberta,	from	my	hon. friend'sconstituency of Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), Mr. David Hayes. I hope that the new minister will study carefully the proposals made by David Hayes of the Canada Land and Irrigation company. This man has given splendid service to this country in that dry belt. With the expenditure of a few million dollars he could continue his present irrigation	programme up	to	the	environs ofMedicine Hat. Anyone who wanted to see what a dried-out area is needs only to go west from Medicine Hat. I went over the area very carefully last summer. It would break one's heart to see the abandoned houses and barns and to think of the effect that it must	have on that	fine	city	of MedicineHat.	What an effect	it would	have if those
works west of Medicine Hat were completed and, instead of there being 200,000 acres of non-irrigated land growing nothing, they were irrigated, as they could be and made productive if the Canada Land and Irrigation company were given assistance. A non-productive area adds nothing to the national wealth of the country. But an area producing all sorts of crops that could be produced with the help of irrigation water which is available if we would only store it and convey it, means additional national wealth and much employment besides.
I must hurry along. The Canadian Manufacturers' association made a submission to the senate committee. Their submission asked several important questions. I think the Prime Minister alluded to the sum and substance of them. I shall place them on Hansard. No. 1 was as follows:
To what extent will other countries abolish import and exchange restrictions and quotas and reduce their customs tariffs? There has been some talk of this but as yet no action.
2.	To what extent will exchanges be stabilized? For example, what might be the effect of the comprehensive proposals announced recently by the British and American governments for the stabilization of exchanges?
3.	Many of our members have greatly increased their exports through imperial preferential tariffs. What is to be the future of these preferences?
4.	To what extent will the system of lend-lease be continued after the war?
Therefore the Prime Minister was quite right in referring to conditions that might take place after the war. The members of the Canadian Manufacturers' association submitted those possibilities, and of course everything is predicated upon what can be done. I understand that the two to three thousand manufacturing plants in Toronto have already made plans for about $95,000,000 worth of additions in buildings alone, but to equip those buildings

Department oj Reconstruction
as they should be equipped will mean the investment of another $225,000,000 in machines and tools. Just fancy what that will mean after the war to the tool manufacturing companies throughout eastern Canada, which to-day are running full blast on war production. I have said before, but it is worth repeating, that if we all get together and do our part to see that men and women obtain employment after this war, by developing this country, there need not be any unemployment.
I should like to speak for a moment or two on one other matter. In addition to new buildings and equipment and the development of natural resources, there are in all parts of the country projects which I could name, if it were not for wearying the house, which would provide employment for hundreds of thousands of men. I could mention projects from Cape Breton right across the country to Vancouver and Victoria, east to west and south to north for a thousand miles; just lying there, waiting for the work to be done which will not only provide employment but open up this country. That is what we want.
I wish to say a word about the human element. I was greatly struck by an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star of May 29. According to the Star it might be inferred that the magnificent performance of the Russians in driving the Germans back from Stalingrad, and the Russians' marvellous feats of fighting, could be the result of the physical training thev were given before the war. I am going to suggest that the new minister of reconstruction bring in a programme of sports and physical exercises, and I do not mean sport just for the fun of it but sport for the development of the physique of Canadians, so that they may receive the benefits of good physical training. According to this report, in 1914 the Russians had only 250 sports clubs with about 30,000 members; but as they saw the marvellous contributions made to the life of their nation by strong men and strong women, they introduced physical culture classes into their universities; they began to train instructors, and by 1940 they had 50,000 sports clubs of one kind or another, fifty technical schools training instructors, and physical culture classes in universities. As a result they have been able to do things we never conceived they would be able to do when war broke out. We in Canada can do likewise, and in so doing create a great deal of business. I do not know if we have been told how much business and employment a huge physical programme would give, but just think for a moment what would result if we had 10,000 clubs in Canada training young men in all kinds of good, healthy sports, such as baseball, football,
hockey, running, and so on. Think what that would mean in equipment. I saw some figures on this matter, but unfortunately I do not have them with me. In addition to the monetary side of the picture, however, I am sure the country would greatly profit from the development of the physical life of our people.
Then, just to give an idea of what can be done, a short time ago I had the privilege of visiting a very great friend of the Prime Minister, Jack Miner. He suggested a programme of rehabilitation which I have not heard mentioned by anyone else. The work he does at Kingsville, Ontario, in connection with wild life conservation brings thousands of tourists and creates a good deal of employment. He said to me, " Why could we not have all over Canada sanctuaries such as I have here; in Alberta, in Saskatchewan, in northern Ontario, away up in Athabaska, and so on?" That would provide employment; that would give training to the people, and1 I thought it was a very happy suggestion.
Mr. GRAYDON [DOT] He is in a class by himself.

speechtext:
Yes, I can tell my hon. friend that Jack Miner is one of the greatest men living to-day, in any country. I have in my hand a pamphlet published by the national association of manufacturers of the United States from which I should like to quote two or three sentences in conclusion. The pamphlet is entitled "Jobs-Freedom-Opportunity" and reads in part as follows:
By jobs we mean regular employment at productive work for everybody able and willing to work-jobs which provide good working conditions and pay fair wages for the work done, jobs which produce those things and give those services which people need, jobs 'which we select of our own free will and are free to change if we wish-in a word, jobs which create the welfare and prosperity necessary to protect ourselves, our families, and our nation in the years and generations to come. . . .
By freedom we mean the right to live under a government which is the servant, not the master, of the people-without fear that a dictator or his henchmen will control us, watch our actions, listen to our words, tell us what to read, where to live, what to buy, where to work, whom to marry, who our friends can be. Freedom, the freedom for which we are fighting, is the freedom which enables us to choose for ourselves, to make our own decisions. . . .
By opportunity we mean the chance to work and get ahead under our own steam, the chance to plan for our own future, to raise our children with assurance that they can grow and learn and live with that self-respect which is the right of free men.
That is the right of free men. Jobs of a hundred and one different kinds must be available. That is why I rise to support the proposal to set up a Department of Recon-
Department oj Reconstruction

struction. I hope the minister of that department will follow out the suggestion which has been made, that of coordinating his plans, and getting things under way now. Let him engage engineers and draftsmen of one kind and another to have the plans coordinated, so that when the war is over he will be able to send men here and there and everywhere. That does not mean that he must take men from Ontario and sen/i them to the west. No; that would not be necessary. Let him give the west a chance to live. If a number of things are done, one of which I have mentioned-and I shall mention others later on, on another occasion-and if the west is given a chance, the people of the west will become buyers. They will send to the east-to here, there and everywhere throughout Canada-orders which will provide thousands of men in the east with jobs in factories.
Let us give every part of Canada a chance to live. I am one who says that we have not given the west a fair chance. I shall not say anything further on the point at this time. May I state briefly that I am behind the proposal to set up a ministry of reconstruction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking to this matter of reconstruction I would be untrue to myself if I were not immediately to put on record some of the thoughts already expressed by me to audiences outside the House of Commons respecting the manner in which the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment has carried on its work.
As has been said before, the members of that committee come from every geographical division of Canada. They are representative of practically every school of political thought in the land; and yet at no time did party politics ever intrude, or cast its shadow across our discussions and deliberations. As chairman of that committee may I express to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) my appreciation not only of the words he used to-day when referring to the committee, but of the manner which he, as Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council, and his government have given consideration to the various recommendations contained in the reports of that committee.
When the Prime Minister spoke he referred in eloquent terms to the nature of the work accomplished by the expenditure of money during a time of war, and he contrasted the expenditure of money in war time with the expenditure of equal or necessary sums of money for peace-time purposes. In view of what he said I should like to read part of [Mr. MacNicol.l
one paragraph from the report of the committee, which was tabled by me in June, 1943. We said:
When war is over some other definite aim must take its place as a motivating cause of national economic activity. Thoughts of those who return to us from the field of battle and of the dependents of those who die, and of what they fought and died for, will supply the aim. Your committee is certain that the means of doing so will be found in the conservation and proper utilization of our natural resources, and in the decision that markets will be sought for our production by governmental intervention where necessary from time to time. In this respect we welcome the conclusion arising from the united nations food conference that never again will food be destroyed simply because people have not enough money to buy it.
A little later in the few minutes during which I shall address the house-because I intend to close at six o'clock-I shall make reference to the manner in which money may be procured, if emergency should arise. Before doing that, however, I would turn to some other matters, and would deal first with a further statement appearing in the report of the committee in January:
Your committee feel that it is well within the power of governments and industry to maintain full employment for all Canadians during the period of transition from war to peace-time activities.
Then we went on to deal with the provisions which must be-I was going to say "ought" to be, but I believe "must" is the better word- made for the returning veterans. In that connection I would call the attention of the house to paragraph (e) of section 2 of the bill, where we find the definition of the word "reconstruction". It says:
"Reconstruction" means the reestablishment in civil life and reemployment on demobilization of the men and women of the armed services, of persons released from war industries, and the reorganization of industry, in order to provide maximum production and full employment during and following the change-over from war-time production of industry to peace-time production, and includes every undertaking by dominion, provincial or municipal authority or by any corporation or other person which may contribute to such reorganization.
I agree with the Prime Minister as to the change he suggested in the explanatory note, but it would be difficult to give to the department duties of a more general or more onerous nature. This, therefore, is a recognition of the fact that the government realizes and is determined to carry out every step necessary to maintain economic activity in the days of peace. The definition includes the two phases set out to-day by the Prime Minister, namely, those of domestic and international economies, depending upon trade and

Department oj Reconstruction
commerce which, in turn, depend upon the relations between Canada and other nations of the world.
The Prime Minister made a brief reference to the fact that the conduct of Canada during this period of war has been a sort of preface to the work which must necessarily be done by Canada in days of peace. I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members the truth of that statement. We have debated, and there has been discussed in the country, the question of mutual aid, and all it implies. I shall not go into details in that matter. This mutual aid policy has built up in favour of Canada an extremely good feeling among those allied nations in the company of which Canada is fighting this war against Germany and Japan-and formerly against Italy.
Then we must consider the conduct of the war, as it is carried on partly by civilians, governmental officials and others, and especially by the youth of Canada who to-day and for some years past have been fighting the battles of those of us who must remain at home. The nature of the struggle they have been carrying on is such that when, the war being over, a minister of the crown or a government official comes to deal with officials of other nations with a view to bringing about trade and commerce or any other interrelation, he will have had the way paved for him by the courage and determination of our young men and women who are fighting our battles overseas to-day and who in the future will be fighting on the Pacific against Japan.
While trade and commerce are absolutely essential to the maintenance of a full economy, I believe that, regardless of the good relations we hope and feel assured will be ours when the war is done, we can never be certain of the nature and course of entangling alliances when the war is over. We hope for the best, and so long as the present Prime Minister is at the helm of affairs those relations will be of the best. My point is that, regardless of what we may attain by international trade and commerce, it is the supreme duty of the government and this house to make certain that in any event our domestic economy will be in proper condition from the time this war ends, and for all the time following.

I sincerely hope, and I feel positive not only from conversations with the Prime Minister and his ministers but from the wording of this bill, from which time will not permit
me to quote much, that the government of Canada are determined that the moment the war is over, at long last they are going to give the agricultural population of Canada that for which they have been striving for generations. The evidence of that is to be found not only in this bill, but in the Farm Improvement Loans Act, in all the facilities for credit for agriculturists, in the determination that from now on those who are engaged in agriculture in all its branches shall be put in the same position as men who gain their living in other branches of our economic system.
In speaking of agriculture I must not neglect to say a word for the branch which is concerned with cattle and live stock generally. I throw out this strong warning-if I may use that word-to the Prime Minister, that as soon as the war in Europe is over

by which I mean that we must reach this point before we have finished the war with Japan-this government must act with dispatch and with energy to make sure that the cattle-men of Canada are once more given that free access to the markets of the United States which the Prime Minister, through his own work, secured for them in the late fall of 1935 and renewed in 1938. Those cattle-men have not this market to-day. They are accepting the situation because of the conditions of war, but we must make certain that that market is returned to them at the earliest moment when war conditions are such that there is no reason why the United States boundary should be closed to our live stock producers.
Another thought occurs to me in connection with agriculture; it relates to secondary industry as well, but for the moment I am dealing with farming. A budget is now in course of preparation. I am making no definite recommendations with respect to it, but I call to the attention of the Ministry of Finance (Mr. Usley)-and I do so now because in this bill we are preparing for the days of reconstruction-that farmers generally, but perhaps cattle-men especially, have paid a severe ratio of taxation. The period before 1935 was a time when they had no markets; their market in the United States was opened in 1936; and the period of three or four or five years immediately before the war included some very lean years, when they were selling cattle in my Cariboo country for one to one and a half cents a pound, while at the same time we were paying seventy-five cents to eat a piece of that cattle-meat in the way of steak at a meal. The amount of money which our farmers have on hand-or have not on hand-* to put into their business is going to make a huge difference to the way in which they can enter the era of reconstruction.
Department oj Reconstruction

I have mentioned the ability to finance those things which must be done. We all know that we cannot properly build up agriculture without the expenditure of money; we cannot maintain industry at a high level without the expenditure of money either by private industry or by government. So that I shall not be misunderstood, may I state quite definitely, although I do not think it is necessary, that I am not a socialist; I am a believer in free enterprise. I realize, however, that free enterprise is meant to embrace the ordinary common man, whether he be a small business man, a farmer or a fisherman, as well as the operators of big business enterprises and those who derive their profits therefrom. The profits which some of our small business men, some of our fishermen and some of our farmers have obtained from their operations have not been commensurate with what they have put into their businesses. That is particularly true of the farmer, because the farmer not only puts money capital into his business, but he puts into it his whole life and the lives also of his wife and children, and the profits-I use the word advisedly, because those who engage in business must have profits-accruing to the farmer are not commensurate with the work and the capital which he puts into his operations.
In dealing with expenditures of. money I have said on many occasions-sometimes I have been laughed at for saying it; sometimes not-that if in the future we were at any particular moment faced with an emergency which would bring about a lack of production and a shutting down of industry through the creation and operation of fear in the minds of the people who are running industry, under our present banking system-and I am not saying anything for or against the banks-if an emergency of that kind threatened in the days of reconstruction, through the operation of the central bank we could without any trouble bring about an expansion of credit which would take care of the situation and drive the emergency from us.
When we bring about that expansion of credit, whether we should accompany it by heavier taxation and heavy borrowings such as is being done during the war would be determined by the circumstances of the case. The thought I am giving out is this, and I am doing so from my place in the House of Commons because I am convinced that there is in the minds of many, many thousands of the people of Canada a dread that when the incentive of war has left us, the conditions that confronted us ten years ago will be back with us again. Many of us who are here know that that will not take place again, but it is
[Mr. Turgeon.l
one of our supreme duties and responsibilities to make certain that the people of Canada, and especially those of our youth who are overseas in our armed services, know that we have determined that it never shall happen again, and know at the same time that -we have at our disposal the means which our good will can put into force to make certain that their fears in that respect will never be realized.

I am not talking of the
past but of the future. The Prime Minister touched on this matter wThen he addressed the American Federation of Labor convention in Toronto a year ago and said that we had learned lessons from the experiences of the war, that we now know what we did not know of some things that can be done to avoid a recurrence of such times. I am pointing out now what can be done, provided that those in authority have the will to do it, and then we can rest easy because we have the means at our disposal.
I have not many minutes left, Mr. Speaker. There are several things of which I wish to speak, but I shall mention only two. There

Department oj Reconstruction
has been some discussion to-day of the federal-provincial conference dealing with reconstruction. A conference is a necessary step, and here I want to give a word of warning to the heads of all governments in Canada, federal and provincial. I do so as a citizen and as a private member of the house who through his work on the reconstruction committee, has come in personal contact with many hundreds of men and women from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I warn all governments in this country that they must not let constitutional difficulties, clashes between jurisdictions and ministries, stop them from properly carrying out the work of reconstruction. The people of this land will no longer permit conflicts of jurisdiction between governments and clashing of ideologies to interfere with the people's attainment of a proper living atmosphere.
Just a word on housing. I think the national housing legislation which has been in operation for some time, and particularly before the war, did a great deal of good, but the good which it did was confined largely to the big cities where the lending institutions had their offices or agencies. There were innumerable towns and villages distant from the big cities that did not get much benefit from that housing legislation, because the lending institutions did not have their agencies established in the rural areas. Therefore I hope that when the legislation which I *understand is now in preparation comes down it will contain provisions empowering the government to make certain that the good arising from the operation of the National Housing Act will be extended also to families that live in towns and villages in rural areas where the lending institutions do not maintain agencies.
My last thought relates to a matter which I dislike to bring up, but it must be considered and my viewpoint upon it must be given. I am thinking now of the Japanese, and this touches a very important part of the whole problem of reconstruction. I do not intend to say much about the Japanese themselves, except to repeat what I have already said in this house, that I am utterly opposed to the return of the Japanese to British Columbia and I am in favour of sending them to Japan when the war is over.
May I speak in complimentary terms of the government and of the House of Commons and of the Senate for the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act, which was given to us two or three years ago through the operations of a committee appointed by this house, and whose chairman (Mr. Macmillan) I see sitting to my left near the Speaker. The Veterans' Land Act provides that the veterans of this war who desire to go into
fishing may receive financial assistance in the same measure as those who wish to go into farming. At the end of the last war an amendment was moved in this house making that very suggestion. It was an amendment to a report from a committee, but that amendment was not accepted. I am proud to say that the mover of that amendment was Colonel Cy Peck, of British Columbia, a Victoria Cross, man, then member for my neighbouring constituency of Skeena, and the seconder was my father, from the province of New Brunswick, who in spite of his age is still watching the proceedings of this house. The point I wish to make is this. Had that amendment been accepted and the veterans of the last war been given financial assistance to go into the fishing industry we would not have had in British Columbia the tragic situation of having the fishing industry almost entirely under the control of the Japanese at the time the attack on Pearl Harbor took place; and we would not have had the further circumstance that when Pearl Harbor was smashed the Japanese naval authorities had as much knowledge of the Canadian western Pacific at that time and for a couple of years following Pearl Harbor as our own naval authorities had. I leave this thought with the members of the government and the members of the house, that good attains its own end and brings its own reward. If twenty-five years ago we had given more assistance to the soldiers of the last war we would not have had that tragedy on the Pacific coast of Canada. If during the period between the last war and the beginning of this war we had thought less of money and taxation and more of human, values and the welfare of the veterans of that war we would have been in a better position, spiritually and morally as well as industrially, to meet this war when it began. But I know that no further urging is necessary because the ministers and the members of the house are desirous of doing everything they can for the veterans. But when we think of reconstruction the supreme goal must be the welfare of those men and women who have been fighting our battles for us. When I say welfare I do not mean charity. I mean that we must see that upon their return to us, those who do not die in this war will be able to secure employment suited to their ability and their skill, that they will have a decent standard of living, and that those from whom the rigours of war have taken away the ability to work will have the same standard of living through the continuance and the improvement of the system of pensions and allowance which we now have.

The national dividend is not something for nothing. It is a dividend, a dividend on the profits of a solvent and successful trading community, Canada Unlimited, of which every citizen is a shareholder by birth. The national dividend is payable in addition to whatever income people now enjoy. The national dividend is payable to all and is the same for all. The national dividend is payable whether a man works or whether he does not work, and anyone who cannot make that concession does not believe in freedom. To those who suggest that a universal dividend would demoralize I can best reply in the words of Desmond MacCarthy, who said:
They do not love liberty who fear licence.
It is just as absurd to suppose mankind on the whole uniformly bad as to suppose it uniformly saintly. The evidence is that the more you give people decent conditions of living, the more likely they are to behave like reasonable citizens. To claim that human beings are essentially vile and can be kept within bounds only by .being kept so busy that they have no time to get into mischief is positively a pagan conception of life and should not be tolerated in a country calling itself Christian.
The struggle to overcome difficulties is most ennobling, but we have reached the stage in our economic history when it is no longer necessary for man to consume most of his energies in the mere struggle for existence. Rather than cause harm and injury to society the national dividend will grant Canadians their first opportunity to reach the highest possible state of civilization, which any nation can attain, namely, a leisure state. The leisure state is a physical possibility in postwar Canada. The leisure state is not a loafer's paradise; the leisure state is the opportunity of opportunities for man to give expression to his God-given creative instincts without any coercion by either nature or man. When a man is free to choose his own form of activity he becomes a man of leisure. When a man is compelled to work, by governments or others, he becomes a slave. Because man was made in the image of his Creator the only important business he has on earth is to create. If he is cheated of this opportunity he goes bad; in time the society which contains him goes bad. Nothing compensates human beings for being maimed in this way. The essential task of a stable and healthy society is to produce conditions in which the creative instinct will have the fullest play. This, not TMr. Kuhl.J
the finding of employment, should constitute the major task of Canada's statesmen in the post-war period.
The whole purpose of the power machine is to save work, to provide us with more goods and more leisure. The power machine is God's gift in response to man's quest. Let us beware how we mishandle it. In thinking on this subject one writer has said:
To refuse to allow the machine a free hand is to wantonly throw away the fruits of man's victory over the forces of nature, and he guilty of the foul and heartless blasphemy of flinging the bounty of the earth back into the face of Him who is the "Giver of all good things."
I grant, Mr. Speaker, that it is not possible to enter the leisure state overnight. I am as much aware of the need for a transitional period as are any other hon. members. I am quite aware that we shall be obliged, before the transitional period is over, to expend a good deal of our energies in assisting in the rehabilitation of those countries which have been overrun by the enemy. I quite agree that there must be a transitional period. Nevertheless I insist that the leisure state should be made our objective, and should be attained at the earliest possible moment. The proper use of leisure naturally will be preceded by appropriate education. This involves a complete change in our notions of a proper education. Our present methods of education have one aim, largely; that is, to fit children to earn their living. But our present system of education does not give any attention to the training for leisure, the reason being that it is expected of the greater number of the children 'that , they will not have much leisure. The whole of our life suffers from a lack of balance in our civilization. Because the benefits of the power machine are not distributed we suffer from anxiety, the fear of losing our place in the fierce scramble for jobs, the fear of war, the fear that with age we shall be forced out of the race. Few of us lead lives in which work well done alternates with periods of relaxation. We work all the time, and our work brings us no deep satisfaction. Factory hands are no more than hands; the activity of their minds is stunted and killed off. Those who are mental workers neglect the proper care of their bodies. Once the people of Canada have received the appropriate education they will, in their ample leisure, do those things for which their long education has prepared them. They will build cathedrals, compose music, write books, paint pictures, join in acting plays, carry out scientific research, cultivate their gardens, explore jungles, invent a new type of aeroplane, learn to fly, weave rugs, and learn languages. Every human being brought up in conditions of free-

Department oj Reconstruction
dom and taught to use his mind and body has something to contribute to the common culture, to be handed on to future generations.
The reason why the ancient civilizations of Babylon, Egypt, Crete, Greece and Rome attained such cultural heights was that the citizens were free from the necessity to work for a living. True, these civilizations rested upon a foundation of slavery, and without this economic foundation none of those ancient civilizations would have been possible. All the menial work, the unskilled work and much of the skilled work was done by the slaves. Thus the citizens were set free for service, both military and civil, for the cultivation of the arts and philosophies, for the dignity of the soldier, the magistrate, the artist or the thinker. The fruits of this system are to be seen in the glory that was Athens, which is the wonder and envy of the modern world. Through the incident of war many of our service personnel have had the privilege of witnessing at first hand some of these achievements. In our own day slavery as it was known in the past is gone, and man is nominally free. He has political freedom but not economic freedom. In these days of mechanical power the machine is fulfilling the function of the human slave of olden times. Just as slavery lifted the burden of toil from the backs of the free citizens of that day, so should the machine do now for all the people of Canada as well as the people of every other country in the world. Not only should the people of Canada be able to attain a state of culture comparable with those ancient civilizations; they should be able to surpass them. It is only by reasoned use of our resources to give all men security, leisure and the power to use it to keep themselves in mental and bodily health and balance that we can be saved. When we do this we restore to life a spiritual meaning; we make reverence for life the principle of our common effort.
Such is the condition of society which exservice men and others ought to be permitted to enjoy in post-war Canada. Such is the condition of security with freedom which a social credit economy offers as an alternative not only to what Canadians have been subjected to in the past but also to the possible socialistic, communistic or fascist totalitarian state of the future. The way of life which I have pictured in my remarks is not a utopia, unless of course a utopia be defined as a condition of security with individual personal freedom. I have depicted a way of life which is physically possible in the Dominion of Canada. Its realization is not dependent upon factors which are yet to be determined. The modern slave-the power machine-stands at
the threshold, awaiting our bidding, to provide all I have alluded to. The national dividend is the ticket of admission to the land of promise, the land which others have beheld from afar, but which is ours for the taking. It is the dividend or chaos; the leisure state or the slave state.

Mr. Speaker, in asking for the privilege of speaking to-night from my place in this house, I do so because I am deeply conscious of the possibilities of a part of the country to which I wish to direct the attention of the new ministry of reconstruction. If after the very many able adresses I have heard to-day my remarks appear to be confined to a local issue, may I remind hon. members of the fact that the section of the country I represent is a vast territory in itself, one which has great possibilities and which, furthermore, is the gateway-to the great northland extending for a thousand miles or more to the Arctic ocean. A bountiful Providence has filled that area with immeasurable wealth, as a challenge to our young men when they return and to those who have been unable to go overseas, but have contributed their effort through their activities in the war industry of Canada.
I am deeply impressed with the fact that, although my remarks may be considered to be those respecting a certain region in Canada, the possibilities of that region are such that they make matters affecting it a national issue. There can be no doubt that the wealth which can be derived from that great portion of Canada which extends from the city of Edmonton to the Arctic ocean is, indeed, of national importance.
In justifying my mentioning place names whicih may be unknown to some hon. members, I direct their attention to the fact that every day since the beginning of the war we have learned about new places on the map, places which heretofore were unknown to us but which, because of the advances of our armies, have become vital spots in connection with the winning of the war.
I am impressed by the further fact that, unfortunately, the ordinary private member is unable to acquaint himself, as he might wish, with all parts of this great dominion. Very few of us have the means to travel throughout the length and breadth of this vast territory, in order to become acquainted with its peoples and its possibilities. Therefore I believe I may be pardoned if in the course of my remarks I mention places which may be unknown to some.
In his speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) covered the ground to such
Department of Reconstruction

my heart and in my love of the north country, that country in which I have lived so long. It is inspired by love of its people, so able and courageous, by love of the boys and girls who are now representing us so nobly and heroically on every field of battle, and who will come back to that great north country. Those young men are going as high in the sky as man can reach. From peaceful Canada, which a few months ago did not have a fighting aeroplane, they are now giving odds to the Luftwaffe. Our sailors traversed the seas in winter, when undersea beasts were lurking everywhere, when their ships were covered with ice. To-day the boys of the army are fighting at the doors of Cherbourg, and to-morrow they will be fighting at the doors of Paris and other cities. Do you think that those boys will be afraid of the challenge to go up north and help us develop that great country? It is to be hoped that they will not have been affected by the idea which, unfortunately, some people in this dominion are scattering around, that we are not doing anything, that we are not preparing to take care of those young men. I say this by the way, but I believe those will stand condemned who for political expediency, for the sake of gaining a few votes, attempt to discourage the man who is giving everything he has, who is risking his life, whose bones, it may be, will lie forever in the soil of Europe because he has sacrificed his all for the sake of his country. Let us do nothing which will deprive such men of encouragement. Let us tell him, as it is the truth to tell him, that this country is prepared to do everything on his behalf, and has been so prepared for some time, and that there will be in this country every opportunity for such young men when they come back from overseas; their experience will be invaluable.
Consider what lies north of Fort McMurray. I mention a spot on the map, but I again remind my hearers of the vast spaces which lie there. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that it is farther from Fort McMurray to Fort Norman, where the Americans built that pipeline into Whitehorse, than it is from Winnipeg to Edmonton Do you know that up there in the north of Canada there is an empire in the making? There are no better people in this world than our strong men of the north, meeting the challenge of that great country. The time will soon come when the tremendous water powers of that great region can be harnessed for the service of our country. I have seen the Chaudiere falls and have been told by some hon. gentlemen of the tremendous volume of water that flows down the Ottawa river. But it is but a drop in the bucket compared with the mighty Athabaska

river, the Peace river, the Clearwater river, with all their tributaries eventually falling into one tremendous river dropping hundreds of feet at Fort Fitzgerald. The power is there waiting to be developed in quantities sufficient to meet the needs of all peace activities in the west. It is now lying dormant, but it will not remain dormant long.
I want to congratulate the government upon taking steps to form this new Department of Reconstruction. I know, as the Prime Minister has said, that a lot has already been done on reconstruction. The provinces have all been working on the problem too. The province of Alberta has presented, as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) told the house this afternoon, a very fine programme to the committee on reconstruction, and that province will cooperate in every way with the federal government. Before a committee at Edmonton representations have been made for a bridge across the Athabaska river, at the town of Athabaska, to open up that great north country where already about 1,000 people are living and are at present served only by a ferry to get in and out. Another great bridge has been proposed over the Saskatchewan river at a point south of Elk Point. These projects are before the government of Alberta and will be submitted when the time comes for the governments to consider their reconstruction programmes.
I w'ish the hon. member for Davenport were here. I admire him very much for the able address he gave to the house this afternoon. He mentioned the word "unity". He emphasized how it was necessary for us all to get together both now and after the war. That appeals to me, as it does to every Liberal. It is the one thing we have preached ever since the party existed-unity, unity. We may differ with our hon. friends opposite as to the best means of accomplishing our aims, but there is no need to quarrel or fight among ourselves. There is no need for bitterness. We can all get together with one common aim and purpose. I am too humble a backbencher to pretend to give advice to this honourable chamber. There are too many able men here for me to presume to give them advice. But perhaps I may draw from the experiences I have had, and I would say, Mr. Speaker, that while we might have a market for our wheat at perhaps two dollars a bushel, while we might find a market for all our surplus stock and for all the production of our forests and everything we produce, unless we have that unity which we have been preaching for so long, unless you and I have one common aim and purpose, one love and one love only, the love of the soil of

Department oj Reconstruction
Canada, we cannot have true progress. Surely we should be prepared to spend everything we have to keep the soil of Canada sacred, unsullied by the foot of the enemy. Some may criticize us for spending so much money on the war and for sending our men and women over there, but I wonder how they would feel if the fight were taking place on this soil we love so much. Therefore, let me repeat, let us have one common aim, and one common ambition, the love of our country, no matter whether we were born here or came here and learned to love it. There is one place where we can show our unity, and that is in this new department which is shortly to be organized. I hope that our common aims will be fulfilled one hundred per cent m the reconstruction undertaken under this new department. Again I wish to compliment the hon. member for Davenport upon the noble thoughts he expressed so ably this afternoon when he spoke of unity.
Perhaps I have said enough, Mr. Speaker. It is not very often I take advantage of such an august audience as I have listening to me to-night. I may not be long for this world; we do not know. I may not be long for this house because surprising things happen in politics. We have had a surprise quite recently. But as long as I have the honour and the privilege to sit in this house I shall speak for those who sent me here and give everything I have, every energy and every talent I possess, to this representation.
I have already spoken of the railroad, of the highway, of the power possibilities of the far north. I shall not speak of the gold mines of the north. I am sorry that so few members have visited this great north country of ours. When the war is over and travel is again possible without the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) scolding us, may I invite the members of this house to visit us, to come to the northland, to the great Athabaska valley and sail down the great Mackenzie river. What a sight that will be for hon. gentlemen! What wealth of knowledge you will acquire; what a knowledge of the possibilities of Canada! Most of us are unaware of the possibilities and the wealth that is to be found in that far north country. Come and visit us. It will be a more enjoyable trip and better for your health than visiting any other place in the world. Do not go and see the battlefields, which would only remind you of every drop of blood that has been shed there and of the quivering flesh of our boys fighting in the struggle for freedom. Come to the peace of the great northland.
May I conclude by saying that I once heard a great orator in western Canada. Some of
the old-timers here may remember him. I think the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross) will, and perhaps the hon. member for Davenport, because he came from Toronto. Apparently many good things come out of Toronto. This great orator once described the beauties of our Alberta rivers and valleys. I shall not attempt to give his exact words, but what he said went something like this: The Beneficent Being who threw the world into space and created the sun and the moon and the stars and the planets and sent them all on their orderly courses, in the presence of which marvels we must all feel so humble, after having taken six days to create this beautiful universe decided to take a rest. And having cast a look upon His work He declared Himself satisfied. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that He had at that moment overlooked one of the great valleys of the Athabaska river or the Peace river in the northland of Alberta.

As a member of the reconstruction committee I feel it incumbent upon me to express my opinion on this matter. Listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, when he introduced the bill, I think the most significant part of his statement was very brief. He made it when he was answering a question of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and in doing so I believe he struck the kernel of the whole problem. He stated in that answer that during the process of fighting the war our economy was so organized that many things were possible which might be considered impossible during the days of peace, the reason for that being that all the nations had a common objective while prosecuting the war. I hope that those who will be administering this legislation now before the house, in the period of reconstruction, and similar legislation in other countries of the united nations, will also have a common objective in those days of peace. If we have not a common objective in the reconstruction period, then it is an admission that we are not all fighting the war for the same thing. There is not a reason in the world why in the days of peace we should not carry out the many slogans we hear advanced to-day as regards the reasons for the sacrifices which every nation is making in finance, in materials and in human resources. If those slogans are not realized in the days of peace, then I am afraid that the time is not far distant, in the aftermath of this war, when we shall start another conflict.
To my mind this problem, while many hon. members have advanced different theories which are confusing, and which lead one to

Department of Reconstruction

believe that the road ahead is difficult and that we have many impasses ahead of us, offers no insuperable obstacle. I have no misconception along these lines because in my opinion the problem is very simple. I believe that if to-day we have difficulties in reorganizing our economy on a peace basis, those difficulties are man-made. They will be difficulties owing to the failure of those in control of the nation and of its resources to recognize the impossibility of returning to the conditions that existed in 1939. The mistakes that will wreck the nation will be the -mistakes -made in an endeavour to go back to an era that is already dead. I believe that the war has brought one fact very clearly home to all of us, and that is that the reason why we are locked in battle to-day on the continent of Europe is to be attributed to the failure of the leaders of nations, in the period between the two wars, to recognize the inevitable results of trying to hang on to the old machine without making the necessary democratic and social changes which would have brought relief to the people of all the different nations and so averted armed conflict.
In my opinion the world to-day is lined up in two camps and two camps only. On the one side we have the totalitarian nations which represent the era of the past. They are endeavouring to stop the forces of progress, to turn back the pages of history 500 years by giving us dictators. The democratic peoples of the world who believe in moving forward into freedom within the framework of democracy, and making democratic social changes, changes of the kind that would have made a fundamental difference in the structure of every country in the order of society, are the nations which are lined up on the other side and which are fighting to roll back the forces of retrogression. I believe that is true, that on our home front, on the battle front and on every front to-day where people are free, the issue is not the maintenance of the status quo but the bringing about of fundamental changes in the order of society, which will guarantee to every one of the united nations those social objectives for which we are fighting.
If our boys in Europe are dying for anything it is not for a return to the conditions of 1939, and if we are to avoid such a retrogression then those who will handle the problems of reconstruction will have to make drastic changes in their thinking and bring about the necessary changes in the statutes of the country. They will have to change them drastically in order to achieve the social objectives for which, in my opinion, we are fighting this war. If that analysis is true, the only thing necessary is honesty on the part of those

who will be implementing the reconstruction programme in the aftermath of the war-no selfishness, no thought of political gain, but merely one desire to give effect to the social objectives for which we are fighting this war.

Is that what you told them
at Estevan?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
The hon. member can make his own speech, Mr. Speaker, while I am speaking as a member of the reconstruction committee, I desire not to be interrupted. If the hon. member wishes me to say what I said at Estevan and if this house is prepared to give me the privilege of saying it, I am prepared to repeat it. However, as I pointed out a moment ago, we must have a full recognition of these social objectives. Those who desired to maintain the status quo, those who feared social changes more than they feared Hitlers, are responsible for the war.
As a member of the committee, I had the privilege of sitting in at almost all the meetings since its inception, and I wish to pay a compliment to the chairman of the committee. I found him fair, impartial, capable and endeavouring to do the best kind of job he could with the machinery at his disposal, and I found the committee as a whole nonpartisan, studying the whole problem of reconstruction from the point of view of the evidence presented to it and in the light of what was best for the nation. I have only this criticism to offer. Hon. members will recall that when the committee was set up I said in the house, on the resolution for the constitution of the committee, that in my opinion the machinery provided gave the committee one of the most important jobs delegated by the government to any committee and that that machinery was totally inadequate to handle the problem which they had to undertake. I suggested at that time that there should be coordination between the work of the James committee and the work of the economic advisory committee and the interdepartmental committee on pensions and national health which was handling certain matters pertaining to reconstruction. There should be made available to the general reconstruction committee, as it was to the parliamentary committee, a secretariat through which the evidence presented to the committee could be sifted and a precis given to the members. We could have then perhaps brought in fuller and more explanatory reports and thereby made a greater contribution to the department that is now being set up than we did.

Department of Reconstruction
I think the machinery that we had at our disposal was inadequate. I know the chairman of the committee was placed in a position where he had to make a digest of the reports himself. Reams and reams of evidence were presented to the reconstruction committee. In my opinion some of it was the most valuable data that any committee in Canada could get. We met every section of society, from the bankers to the trades unions. We met the provinces. All of that evidence is on file. We have it. There is so much of it that it is impossible for the average member who attends to his work in this house even to read it, much less make a digest of it. I think the committee did' as good a job as could be done with the machinery provided for it.
When this bill becomes law I hope that the minister who will administer the department will not fail to take the reports presented to this house, short as they were, and study them. Certain definite recommendations were made with respect to works programmes necessary to the nation in the different sections of the country, programmes that would provide considerable employment in the period after the war. I hope that these reports presented by this committee will be one of the main pieces of evidence that that ministry will study when they are making their recommendations for a programme of works across the country. I am all in favour of setting up the department. I think this is the department that will have most of the headaches in the period of the war. I hope that the machinery will be adequate for the job.
There are many opinions on this matter of post-war reconstruction. I do not pose as an expert on any of the different schools of thought, but I am going to say that I do not agree with those who express the view that all the post-war problems of Canada are dependent upon international machinery that will regulate the economy of this country. I am not in favour of any machinery set up outside Canada that has anything to do with telling the government of Canada what their post-war plans are to be. I think that is the prerogative of tire Canadian government and the Canadian people. The government of Canada should organize and arrange the internal affairs of this country in accordance with the wishes of the Canadian people from whom they will receive a mandate to govern in the post-war period, whatever government that happens to be.
I am a little afraid of the school of thought that states that international machinery is to be set up for the purpose of deciding on a
monetary unit to regulate international trade, and that a supergovernment is to be set up somewhere which is to arrange the flow of materials from nation to nation. If that is followed through to its logical conclusion, all that it adds up to is the kind of thing against which we are fighting to-day, a dictatorship from the outside superimposed on the smaller nations that are fighting the war at the present time. I am afraid of that kind of thing, and I do not think that, while we are fighting a war, with the picture as it is as between nation and nation, when the war itself overshadows everything, when the future is beclouded, Canada or any other country should commit itself to international machinery that will be able to dictate the internal policy of this country after the war. I agree that during the time of fighting the war, for military reasons, it is the prerogative of those who are handling the military affairs of the nation to sit in conference to develop the machinery necessary to win the war; but when that war is over, the duty of arranging the internal economy of the different countries belongs to the peoples of those countries.
Take this matter of foreign trade. Certainly we need foreign trade; certainly we shall have to sell goods, but I think the foreign policy of any country is merely the reflection of its internal policy. Our job is first to put our own house in order. Nations export only their surpluses, and they import to the extent that they do not develop their own economy or to the extent that they have a shortage in certain commodities. The first thing to do is to put our own house in order, to determine what our surpluses are, what we have to import and what we have to export, to establish a standard of living for the Canadian people. When that is done we are in a position to go to other countries, sit in on international conferences and make the best bargain possible for the people of our own country in cooperation with other nations.
I am a little afraid of those who are rushing headfirst into international agreements without a mandate from the people of this country or the peoples of the other nations who are fighting the war. I do not think anyone has the right, regardless of his military position, to sit in a conference on which we are not represented and about which we know nothing, and decide that certain things are to be done with respect to this country and the other country in the period after the war. It is the prerogative of the Canadian people to advise the Canadian government if and when we get the job of fighting the war off our hands.
I am not going to take advantage of this opportunity to go into all the ramifications of
Department oj Reconstruction

reconstruction, but I wish to say this with respect to my own province. The premier of Nova Scotia made a presentation to the reconstruction committee. In that presentation he did not paint a very pretty picture. He was very realistic about the problems. We hear talk about cooperation of province with province. The limitations of the British North America Act is often mentioned. I merely wish to ' say this about the British North America Act. If a constitution that was written seventy-six years ago retards progress in this country, then that constitution should be changed to make for progress. The premier of Nova Scotia pointed out that in so far as he and his government were concerned-and it is a Liberal government in that province- cooperation was a thing that was very hard to get. He suggested that if there is any solution for the problems of the maritimes in the postwar period, decentralization of industry will have to take place. He deplored the trend that is taking place during the war of further milking the maritime provinces of established industries, and that has gone on within the last year or so. He pointed to the closing down of the steel plant at Trenton, the scrapping of the shipyard at Pictou, the closing down of the sugar refinery at Dartmouth, and the closing of the Clark Ruse aircraft plants in Dartmouth and Moncton. If that is to be the trend there is not very much hope for the maritime provinces. Unless there is some definite declaration on the part of the government in the post-war period with respect either to the continuation of the industries that I have just mentioned that have been taken out, or to some programme of creating subsidiary industries in the maritime provinces, then we are only wasting our time and fooling ourselves when we are talking about reconstruction. The time has arrived when we should show our people that we have those plans and that we intend to do a certain amount of work.
Another factor that was brought clearly home to us in the three years that the committee sat was the matter of finances. Province after province" made a presentation referring to wonderful works programmes, striking at the basic problems in each province. Each of the premiers wound up his statement with the same plea: "This is all contingent upon the federal government making available to each province the finances necessary to carry this through." The construction industry and other industries made presentations, all winding up with the same statement: "This is all contingent upon the federal government making available the necessary finances." What does it all add up to? In my opinion it shows that the trend

to-day is toward greater responsibility on the part of the federal government in the matter of finance, in the matter of developing our natural resources. If those natural resources are to be developed by the federal government, as was suggested by various agencies that appeared before the committee, then there is great necessity for some control by the federal government over currency and credit. In my opinion that will be one of the main points in the post-war period; unless you have some say over currency and credit in the country you will not be able to expand the economy of the country. If the chartered banks are to say where the money is going, and in what volume, that will strangle your post-war development. I am not going into that matter; we have discussed it in the house already, but I am leaving that thought with the government. It has been made clear to me that this will be one of the limiting factors in the development of our resources in the aftermath of this war.
When this bill is in committee I intend to discuss it clause by clause, but for the moment I merely wish to leave this suggestion with the Prime Minister and the government. Everyone I hear discussing the problem simply creates more confusion. We hear many platitudes; we are told the things that cannot be done and the limitations that exist. As I said in the beginning, there are no limitations except an honest desire on our part to see this programme through. I have in my hand a newspaper clipping which I wish to read; it is very short, but I think it points the way for us if we are not afraid of social change, if we are not afraid to make the necessary fundamental changes in our order of society, if we are not scared by the name socialism. I said that the old machine had broken down; it is dead, but it refuses to be buried. Personally I believe that the war means the funeral of the capitalist system. I am going to read this newspaper clipping for the benefit of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), because it happens to be from the Regina Leader-Post of May 28, 1944. I do not think anyone would ever accuse the Leader-Post of being a socialist organ; I have read a few of its editorials, and I should be inclined to believe that it was rather capitalistic. I read this because I suggested that definite, fundamental changes must be made, not just patches,, palliatives or platitudes. They are not going to change anything. We are living in a world that is real. The problem is an economic problem. The war itself is not theoretical. It is practical; it is real; it is there. It is a problem with which we must grapple, and we are grappling with it. We

Department oj Reconstruction
are fighting it on the battle front. Unless definite social changes are made before the war is over and the eight hundred thousand odd service personnel, the forty thousand women and the million and a half war workers come back to us; if we do not make transitional changes now in a democratic way, while we have the chance, someone will make them for us in a way we may not like. Society will change whether we like it or not; the change will be either evolutionary or revolutionary. While we are wondering, wandering, grasping, debating theories and so on, one country points the way. That country is New Zealand This little clipping, under the date line Vancouver, May 27, reads:
New Zealand's socialist government is a world leader in social legislation, taking care of its citizens from the cradle to the grave, Hon. David Wilson, New Zealand high commissioner to Canada, said in an address to a service club here Friday.
Benefits were in operation for old age, for sickness, for unemployment, for prenatal and maternity care. Cost of living increase of thirteen per cent during the war time was the smallest of any country involved in the present struggle, 'he said.
Then he went on to give a list of the services now being given in that country. All the machinery we have on paper; our social security, our health bill, our reconstruction department, which are merely in the preliminary stages in Canada to-day, are working in that country. If we honestly want to do these things, to bring about such changes, and I believe we do, then we require technical advice on how to go about it. Why, then, is not someone from that country here or someone from this country there making an examination of that programme? All the people of this country want is an honest demonstration that we are not repeating the performances of 1914-18. The slogans we are giving to our people to-day are not new to me. I heard them in 1917 and again in 1919, and during the twenty years between the two wars I travelled with a lamp searching for the implementing of any of those promises. You are not going to maintain an order of society that gave its people three wars in one generation- the Boer war, the war of 1914-18 and the present war, together with a depression the like of which the world had never before seen. You cannot keep that up. That has to be changed, and you are not going to change it on paper, by writing bills or resolutions, by broadcasts or through the Canadian press. You have to give a practical demonstration that you mean exactly what you say.

I do not admit that. We are building machinery from the top, but you do not solve any problem from the top; the machinery must be built from the bottom. If I were the Prime Minister and wanted to be political about it one of the first things I would do would be to establish an old age pension in this country that would offer security to everyone over sixty years of age.
Mr.. MACKENZIE KING: At least I made a beginning, by starting old age pensions.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Yes, but when we established old age pensions we set the age limit too high. W'hat you get at seventy years of age is not an old age pension; and when you have to declare yourself a pauper in order to receive that pension I think it is an insult to the aged people of this country. I am not going to quarrel with the Prime Minister about that; he established the principle, with the cooperation of the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Woodsworth, and the then hon. member for Winnipeg North, Mr. Heaps. This little group takes some of the credit, without going into the history of the thing. My objection now is that the age limit is too high. A man has not long to live after he gets it. Many people do not live long enough to enjoy it. And then before you get it you have to will your second pair of shoes to the premier of the province in which you live. One of the greatest things that could be done1 at this time, one of the greatest political gestures that could be made by the Prime Minister-though I am not suggesting for a moment that he would be political- would be to establish an old age pension for every person in this country over sixty years of age. The first charge against the wealth of any nation should be the care of the aged; those who built the nation; those who gave us the institutions under which we live, those who raise families which fight wars for us, and come back and work in industry for us.

In regard to
old age pensions, did not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) make clear that the government was quite prepared to cooperate with the provinces to bring the age down to sixty-five?
