speechtext:
They are always prepared to do it, but they always throw up a straw man so that we cannot get through it, with the cooperation of the provinces. You hide behind the British North America Act.
Department oj Reconstruction

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but he has referred to New Zealand. I wonder if he has brought out the point that they have only one government in New Zealand, a unitary government, which is able to do things. If there were only one government in Canada the lower age of sixty-five would now be in force.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I appreciate that. I think
we also have one government in Canada. We have a national government in Canada, and that national government passes Che basic laws of the country upon which the provinces can base enabling legislation. There is nothing in the world to stop the federal government- since the outbreak of war, for example-from passing an order in council with respect to this matter. They have passed about 65,000 of them for other matters, and there is not anything in the world to stop them from saying: "Due to the war emergency, when it is necessary to relieve the minds of older people of the burden of continuation of the war, and because of the misery they are going through, we will relieve their minds of the problem of future security; and in that connection we are passing orders in council, and advising the provinces that we are prepared nationally to advise them to drop the age in each province to sixty, and that that pension should be given to every citizen of this country, by right."
We have not a pension by right to-day in Canada. You go before a board and if you have accumulated anything at all-it is a programme of indolence, the way it is administered-you cannot own anything, and you cannot earn anything.
It is absolutely necessary to have that pension at the age of sixty. In the post-war period there will be thousands and thousands who will be coming back and claiming employment. At that time many who have already done their duty should be relieved.
I have been in industry for a long time, and I say it is a sad thing to see an old man crippling out to work-yes, crippling out to work, and I say that advisedly-at five or six o'clock in the morning, and then coming in around five o'clock at night, scarcely able to drag himself home. During the bad years he may have had two or three boys, twenty-four or twenty-five years of age, who were lying around the house, with nothing to do.
Those old men should have been on pensions, and the boys should have been working. Insecurity in old age is one of the greatest detriments of any nation. I am reasonably sure that a large percentage of the people across Canada who are in industry are work-

ing in fear of insecurity. That is one of the things they have in mind-the matter of an old age pension, and knowing that they are not going to wind up their later years on the streets, or in institutions or living on the charity of a son or a daughter, or in the care of friends or relatives.
I am sorry I got into this discussion about old age pensions, but I feel very strongly about the subject. I have seen so many people in the twilight of their lives, people who have made contributions to the nation, left dependent upon charity. Any man who has worked all his life and contributed a family to the nation is a proud man. The workers are proud; they are independent. They do not like to be dependent upon anyone, and they should not be dependent.
We get up and say glibly that the banks are entitled to certain profits by virtue of their making investments with their funds. We say glibly that interest has a right to profits because they sit in their offices and clip coupons. But the worker who goes into the coal mine, or the worker who goes to sea, or the worker who farms the land, and who has put everything he has, including his family, into that work, and who has produced the wealth of the nation, is not entitled to anything. He is not entitled to seek a bite to eat when he is no longer able to work.
You see, that is the trouble with the capitalist system. And all the laws are designed for the capitalist, and to protect him. Nothing protects society itself. That is the difference between socialism and capitalism. Socialism seeks to protect society.
I am sorry I got into this discussion, because I had not intended to do so. I hope that the Prime Minister will pay some attention to and will make some analysis of the thoughts I have tried to express. I am absolutely in accord with the setting up of the department. As a member of the committee on reconstruction I am going to interest myself in that phase of the work; and anything I can do in the post-war period to implement the ideas, recommendations and suggestions which have come out of that committee, I shall consider it my first duty to do.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will agree that next to the prosecution of the war no matter is as important as the problem now under discussion. I was not a little surprised, however, in listening to the speech which has just been delivered, to note the suggestion that the reconstruction of the world should proceed upon the primary consideration of giving to

Department of Reconstruction
each country full supremacy over its economic life. That certainly is not in harmony with the speeches the hon. member, himself, has delivered in this house. Certainly it is not in harmony with the speeches of his leader. Nor is it in harmony with the speech delivered in the city of Ottawa by Mr. Nash, the representative in AVashington of New Zealand.
Certainly the kind of doctrine advocated to-night is the very kind of doctrine which provoked, and did more to bring about this war than any other circumstance apart from the mischievous intentions of Hitler himself.

I would ask my hon. friend to give me the same attention which I gave to him. Undoubtedly this country must, by its own effort-through the effort of this parliament, and the efforts of the various provincial legislatures-do everything humanly possible to give the kind of security of which the hon. member has spoken to-night, the kind of security which every member in the house, interested in the subject, would want to see our people receive.
But let us look at the realities of the situation. We are not living in a Canada of 1867; we are living in an interdependent world, a world which has contracted almost beyond conception. It is a world where one point on the globe is sixty hours from not more than the farthest point. It is a world in which this particular country, traditionally, to the extent of thirty-five per cent of its income, has been dependent upon what it could sell to other nations in the world.
In the face of this situation I am sure the hon. member would agree that the only satisfactory guarantee of real reconstruction in Canada is predicated upon the most successful measure of international political and economic collaboration.

speechtext: The leader of the C.CJF. group has said he agrees with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Undoubtedly that is the situation, and I am not saying this in any political sense. I have talked this sort of thing for twenty years and in some quarters I have been humiliated for doing so. But we have reached the stage in the development of human history where unless the great powers and small powers can arrive at some understanding, not only in regard to political but as well to economic matters, not only shall we not be able to provide at home the kind of security for our people that we want, but we shall set in being again the kind of situation which has provided insecurity and war. Let there be no mistake about that. And this government, not without having made its mistakes, has as its Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a man who recently gave expression in London, at a time and under circumstances which were by no means easy or unanimous, to the conviction that as far as this country was concerned it intended in the projection of its foreign policy to contribute the fullest collaboration in both political and economic matters.
Long before that, in our contribution at the food conference in Virginia about two years ago, in connection with the interim food organization which in consequence has been set up, and in regard to the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration, we gave evidence that not only do we want to have security for our people at home but we recognize our obligation in providing security for other countries and other peoples, realizing that in doing so we are at the same time giving a full guarantee of security for our own people. Recently, at the twenty-sixth meeting of the International Labour Conference at Philadelphia, the government of this country, in cooperation with workers and employers, subscribed, along with the united nations and associated powers then assembled, to the kind of policy which my hon. friend has been speaking about to-night, the desirability of giving to the undeveloped areas of the world in addition to the more fortunate nations the kind of social standards and social security which we in this country want and which, I believe, regardless of political interests, we ultimately shall have; recognizing however there, as we did-not only Canada but the forty-three nations assembled -that we wanted to provide a minima of security, and if that could not be obtained by
Department of Reconstruction

resorting to measures which were traditional, then measures which were untraditional, measures which were not part of the status quo, must be resorted to in order to provide people with the opportunity of full life.
I am sure that the hon. gentleman, on reconsideration, will recognize that he overstated the ease or stated it in a way that he really did not intend.
The problem of reconstruction, it seems to me, falls into two broad categories. First, measures for making the transition from war to peace, when the time comes, as rapidly and smoothly as possible and with the least possible social cost. With regard to this transitional period the government has been alive to the problem. First, we have resorted to the very technique which hon. gentlemen opposite have suggested, for many years-the technique of preparation, the technique of planning. The war had no sooner begun than the James committee and ancillary committees were set up to deal with the problem factually, to understand what that problem was. That technique was in harmony with the kind of planning which hon. gentlemen opposite so often espouse and suggest. The time has come, of course, when these studies, these factual presentations, must be borne in mind and implemented. That is exactly what we are doing to-night in the setting up of a ministry to coordinate, to centralize, to harmonize the action of municipalities, of provinces and of the federal government, based upon the studies which have been made. What better, what sounder, what other sensible course could possibly be resorted to?
During the war, with regard to the problem of transition, the government has had in its very war policies this kind of problem in mind. Its war-time fiscal policy, the price ceiling, controls over production and the allocation of commodities-all have been directed to making an orderly transition possible. They have had the effect, in conjunction with unemployment insurance and the fiscal policy, of building up very great reserves of purchasing power to meet the needs of this period. When you consider that the unemployment insurance fund, now a little more than $200,000,000, built up since 1941 on contributions from the state, employers and workers, will provide in this period of transition, when undoubtedly we shall be faced with the difficulty of keeping men in gainful employment, as we must do, a very useful cushion and one which we shall be pround of having set up.

speechtext: That is the programme.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
The programme is not one of having men out of work. My hon. friend should be serious. He laughs. I do not want to laugh about this thing, and I am sure he does not. This government is setting up a reconstruction ministry. It proposes to set up measures which the hon. member had in mind when he spoke earlier. To suggest that the unemployment fund will not last six weeks is to suggest that everybody will be out of work, which obviously would not be the case. All I am saying is that this fund, of which we all should be proud, will be one of the cushioning factors in the transitional period. I have said no more about it and no less. Then the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply in bringing about arrangements for the termination of contracts and for eliminating delays in industrial reorganization is all part of this policy. There is the provision for the disposal of war assets, for the Industrial Development bank, for our employment services. Our greatly extended arrangements for the retraining of military personnel and civilian workers which have been undertaken under the Vocational Training Act will be of tremendous value in this transitional period. One contemplates, Mr. Speaker, that over 300,000 people have thus far taken advantage of our vocational training. One considers in that amazing record-excelled, incidentally, by no other country of the united nations-the great possibilities of that kind of training to fit men for particular jobs in industry, both in the transitional and in the long-term period.
So that it is not fair, it is not true to say that this government has not, during the war itself, prior to the setting up of this ministry, devoted itself to the fullest consideration of this problem. Only this afternoon I was reading a publication issued by the Fortnightly Review, an analysis of the work of the various governments of the world with regard to this problem of reconstruction. The Prime Minister held up for our scrutiny to-day the publications of the various committees which have been working on this problem, and these publications have received at the hands of the

Department oj Reconstruction
Fortnightly Review in its summary a tribute that no other studies were as complete or as penetrating or as far-reaching as these.
The job, I quite agree, is to go beyond the period of study, to implement these recommendations, and that is the sort of thing we are dealing with here to-night, and with which I want to have something in a very special way to say.
Before doing that, let me say that I recognize that the second phase of reconstruction is the putting into effect of long-term run measures on the need for which public opinion has crystallized. There I agree with the hon. gentleman, as I think every member of the house does. That was reflected clearly at Philadelphia when forty-three nations representing various governments and various shades of public opinion gathered together, and where underlying the deliberations of that conference as undoubtedly representing public opinion of the peoples of the world there was the thought that what we have been able to do during the war in providing a high level of employment must be done during the peace. But it will not be of any help to say that the problem can be done simply. It cannot be done simply. But it is one that must be done. To say that it is simple is to overlook all the international entanglements and difficulties in a country like Canada with its currently inefficient constitutional distribution of powers. But that it must be done I fully agree. One of the things that must be done is to recognize, as the hon. gentleman has recognized and as I do, that under the present distribution of powers in this country, powers extended to the provinces on the one hand and to the federal government on the other, there do not reside in this parliament at the moment the powers that are necessary for giving us the opportunity of dealing with some of the problems that will have to be faced.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I challenge that statement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
The hon. member is a better constitutional lawyer than I am. All I can do is to give my humble opinion. But this government has not overlooked the desirability of taking unto itself powers that now reside elsewhere. It attempted that in 1941, the first real attempt ever made in this country, by having a conference with the provinces in this very chamber, to try to bring about some of the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report, with the idea of stream-lining, if you like, our legislative machinery, with the idea of rendering our legislative powers more efficient. Then, not having succeeded in that conference, it is now
proceeding to another; and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said to-day, steps and preparations are now under way for the holding of another conference between the dominion and the provinces.
While it might be constitutionally possible for us to change the constitution right here and now, one has to consider many other factors. One has to consider that we are a federal state, and if these things can be done by way of cooperation and by way of courtesy, that is the effective way of bringing about the necessary changes. We had a good example of that last December when the dominion Department of Labour met with the provincial departments in a conference, as a result of which certain labour regulations were promulgated. That conference, properly timed and properly prepared, resulted in a great deal of understanding and a great deal of good between the provinces on the one hand and the dominion on the other. I believe that following that model, placing before the provinces the difficulties as we see them and as they undoubtedly see them, it will be possible to arrive at financial measures without which many of these things cannot be done, and at the same time to endow the federal authority with undoubted and undisputed power to deal with matters affecting the social security of our people. That will undoubtedly be one of the matters which will come for the consideration of the future minister of reconstruction.
I should like to say something arising out of my connection with the Department of Labour. I have recognized, as I believe this house will recognize, and I have recognized all during my time in this house the need for a better understanding between labour on the one hand and management on the other. We have recognized officially in this country under the aegis of the War Measures Act the desirability of telling employers that their workers are entitled to sit down with them and to bargain in their own interests. Surely that question has now been removed from the Canadian scene. Any employer who takes the position that he will not bargain with the men who work for him is not only running counter to the law but running counter to what is now the sound social judgment of this country. The disputes connected with union recognition, collective bargaining-all these things I trust are now matters of history.
But there is an opportunity for industry,
and in this it seems to me a ministry of reconstruction will have something to do and something to say, or should have. No longer can anyone look upon industry as simply a profit-motive organization. That is not the view of this government. That is not the view of the

Department oj Reconstruction

Prime Minister of this country, the leader of this government. I doubt if you will find any better definition of the place of industry in modern society than the statement made by the Prime Minister in this house two or three years ago when he said:
Industry is, or ought to be, in the nature of social service. It is not merely a system whereby capitalists may increase profits, or workers find the means of gaining a livelihood through wages. There is the right of the community which makes possible the carrying on of industry and it is reasonable to expect to have the interest and well-being of the community and its members considered in the rewards of industry. In other words, industry exists to serve a social end, as well as to serve the needs of individuals.
That statement represents my feelings as fully as any statement I can find.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What does it mean?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
It means simply this, that industry does not exist and must not in the future be considered to exist as merely an opportunity foT providing profit for those whose interest is in the investment class. In other words, it means that industry exists for the production of goods and for the providing of income and satisfactory standards of living for all of those who share in its operations. That is why it seems to me that a ministry of reconstruction should undertake in conjunction with the Department of Labour, which is now in the process of doing that very thing, to extend the principle of management-labour production councils into a greater democratization of industry. There is no reason why the workers in my own community, for instance, in an industrial city, should not have the privilege of sitting down with management to discuss matters that concern not only the workers themselves directly but matters with respect to the operation of industry, with regard to the fixing of prices of this commodity or of that, and going beyond that, in respect of a more satisfactory income, a greater reward for labour because it, too, makes its contribution to the operations of industry. Some may say that that is going very far; others may say that it does not go far enough. But in my personal judgment it is one of the next steps that we shall face, and I am glad to think that in saying that industry represents a partnership, not only in terms of labour and management but in terms of the distribution of the income of industry, I am expressing the view which my own leader, the Prime Minister of this country, expressed and for which he was for many years severely criticized. I feel that we should extend this principle of the partnership of industry to many of the things we do.

I had dinner to-night with a prominent trade union leader from my own city, a director of one of the biggest trade union organizations in this country. He laid before me the plans of his union, plans that are now in process, with respect to the post-war possibilities of a particular industry with which he is connected. It was not an emotional thing. It was not the approach of an amateur. The union had enlisted some good economists, some experts in the field of taxation, experts in the field of export trade, who are helping the union in trying to devise ways and means of improving its lot in the post-war period and making sure that the men work every day, eleven months in the year, allowing possibly for one month of retooling. That is the constructive approach, and I trust that this ministry of reconstruction, along with the Department of Labour, which is now trying to encourage that sort of thing, will find it possible, not merely in one particular plant, but duplicating the same thing throughout the country, to encourage the employers to sit down with the workers, having before them a carefully prepared document on post-war possibilities for industry. The curious thing is that in this particular case the industry went to the University of Toronto to engage certain economic experts to do the very same job, only to find that the union had beaten them by seven months. I mention this only to indicate what I firmly believe to be the function of government in regard to this matter. The ministry of reconstruction, alive to its job, can encourage that sort of thing, and the benefits would be incalculable.
There are other directions which this ministry of reconstruction can take. What will be the situation when hostilities have ceased? We shall find plants now engaging thousands of men cut off from war contracts and faced with the problem of a heavy surplus of labour. These men will have to be given work, and if work cannot be provided for them in the community in which they happen to be located at the moment; if work cannot be provided through the system of selective service and other agencies, then these, men should be given opportunities elsewhere, wherever they may be, through a policy of decentralization of industry such as my hon. friend has spoken of, through possibly the industrialization of rural life by means of chemurgical opportunities, and so on. Whether these things are imaginary or not, they are bold enough to capture the imagination and to invite the future Minister of Reconstruction to approach the problem with that kind of desire behind his every act. The job will be not only to give men work but to make sure that they work for a sufficiently long period in the year.

Department oj Reconstruction
With the technical skill which we have developed in industry, working for a short time in the year will not be tolerated by the people of this or, I believe, of any other country. That is one question which will have to be dealt with.
Then there will be the question of the transfer of surplus labour and the encouragement of industry from the point of view of location. At present, if an industry wants to come into a particular city it goes and sees the chamber of commerce and discusses the matter with the member of parliament or the mayor. It seems to me that in a properly developed community, a community in which proper and adequate preparation has been made, the ministry of reconstruction would be able to give advice to an incipient industry as to where it should locate, where it would be of the greatest economic value to the community and to the country at large, always of course bearing in mind the question of costs. These, however, will be details which I am sure will be borne in mind by the vigilant ministry of reconstruction which I envisage and which will be established.
The new ministry will deal with other problems which will be of vital importance and which will challenge the imagination of the man who happens to be minister. First of all, there will be the necessity of dealing with such questions as the educational and occupational background of the members of the armed forces, because that information will be essential. We are going to give the members of the armed forces that place in our economic society to which they are entitled. Secondly, the ministry will have to consider information as to the workers likely to be laid off for any length of time in the dismantling of war industries. The Department of Labour at the moment is engaged upon some important surveys in that respect which are proving illuminating and which, carried on more extensively, will be very helpful. In the third place, the ministry will have to consider the probable number and occupational distribution of older workers likely to be retired at the end of the war. It will have to determine the question of labour requirements. It will have to consider the use of government plants for peace-time purposes. It will have to consider the adoption of programmes for post-war employment, such as the building industry. It will have to take action with respect to the demobilization of war industries, guidance and the training and employment of disabled veterans, the planning of public works and so on.
So that the man to whom is entrusted this tremendous task will be faced with a challenge, but he will also have a great opportunity.
I believe that in the minds of every member in the house is the sincere desire to be able to contribute in some way to the bringing about of what is called full employment or a high level of employment in the country. I am satisfied that no longer will our people go and receive a dole without at the same time receiving work for which they will be remunerated. Our people will not want to subscribe to the doctrine of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl).

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: How do you know?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Our people believe in the dignity of work. They do not want to be idle. They want to have an opportunity to work so that they can develop their own personalities and help in the development of the personalities of those who depend upon them.

So you gave them
box-cars. They rode the rods.
Mr. MARTIN.:	The hon. member speaks
of riding the rods. I am arguing against riding the rods. If the hon. gentleman will learn the art of patient listening, I have just stated that our people are not opposed to work. We believe in the dignity of work; and no government, no matter what its political affiliations, will stand for one moment unless it is able to provide the kind of work for our people to which they are entitled.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What happened before the war?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: But that does not mean maintenance of the status quo. The hon. member for Cape Breton South seemed to suggest that we on this side stood for the status quo.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Not all of you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I certainly do not, nor does this government.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What change are you making?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Look over the record of
this government since the war and you will find that we are not the champion's of that form of so-called free enterprise, which has not existed for eighty-five years. We are in the midst of a form of society in which there is a great measure of free enterprise, but there is also a great measure of collective action. To suggest, therefore, that we are status
Department oj Reconstruction

quo'ists, is neither, truthful nor accurate What we honestly believe is this. We believe that we must provide our people with security of employment. If that means the destroying of old labels, then we will destroy old labels. That is the thing. And the very course that we have taken during the war indicates that this government is not tied down but is prepared to experiment boldly, as few countries in the world have experimented, in a manner that surprises many people in the country.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Plunging into debt,
though.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: It seems to me that what we must be prepared to do is to have a very carefully and well planned, well thought out system of public investment working alongside private initiative, taking up the slack where necessary, so that in the days when employment will not, because of its own effort, be up to the highest point, the men and women of the country will be given an opportunity to work, whether it be on the basis of the kind of projects contemplated by the national resources planning board in the United States, or whether it be on the basis of other schemes. I for one, as a member of parliament representing thousands of men, who represent thousands of little children who live in homes that sometimes are not fit to live in, know this. I know they will not tolerate any government or any society that is not prepared to do that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: What will they have to do?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: This government is prepared to do that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: They showed it last August.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: The hon. member insists upon being political with a man who is not inclined to be political. This government is determined-and its actions to-night in proceeding with this bill indicates that-to take steps which perhaps ten years ago would have branded the Prime Minister as radical and dangerous. I am not unmindful of the fact that the present Prime Minister of Canada has been branded before by many men in high places in this country, who look upon him as a kind of dangerous Liberal who is inclined to interfere with conditions as they are and as they would prefer them.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh. The leader of the C.C.F. party, who is
[Mr. Martin. 1
generally responsible in these matters, would I am sure subscribe fully to what I have just said. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in bringing to. a close what I have to say may I observe that in this parliament and in this country we are faced with a challenge. That challenge can be met if we have the same vigilance, the same initiative and the same incentive that during these four and a half years of war have characterized the actions of our people and of all hon. members. We must persist in that. If we want to justify the tremendous sacrifice of men, treasure, and of property that is now taking place in Europe and in other theatres of war, then nothing but the fullest determination to bring this sort of situation about will satisfy. I believe that this government is taking the first step to-night in implementing a programme which it has been considering and planning for many months. The validity of that programme will depend upon the way in which it is attempted to be realized. I have every faith that that implementing will take place. If it does not take place, then, of course, the judgment of the nation will be definite. But on all of us, regardless of our political affiliations, is imposed the most terrific responsibility ever placed upon the shoulders of any legislature, the recognition that in the doing of these things we may be tearing with the past, tearing with things that we have cherished; but nothing is to be gained by taking a doctrinaire attitude and saying that only by resorting to this particular form of government, only under this particular theory can these things be brought about. By providing, through experimentation, by providing for a willingness to change, if the old methods will not do, can these things be brought about.
I believe that there is much in our society that has to go and is going. I do not believe that it is all bad. I believe that we want to try to preserve much that is in it; but all that I am really concerned with is to see that the job is done. I would trust that whoever the Minister of Reconstruction may be, his one objective will be not to be tied down by labels, but to be tied down by one desire, and that is to give to the people of this country, in collaboration with the other nations of the world, those measures without which the full life is not possible.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
When I came into the chamber a short time ago I had no intention of speaking to-night, but having heard the last two speeches I thought that perhaps I should like to comment very briefly upon them.
As I listened to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) to-night, I thought that

Department of Reconstruction
the sound of the Prime Minister's voice of some twenty-five years ago echoed from this chamber. I distinctly remember going to a meeting in the city of Regina in 1919, I think it was, sitting in Westminster church and listening to the first speech I heard from the right hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). At that time he was enunciating to the country the recently adopted programme of the Liberal party. It was immediately following the first great war when in men's minds there was the thought of change and the people thought that the war had been fought for democracy. I distinctly remember that programme. I remember the promise it gave to the young people; I remember the promise it gave to the aged; I remember the promise it gave to the workers and others throughout the country, and I wish to say this, that to-night after twenty-five years most of those promises, as far as social legislation is concerned, remain unfulfilled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Remain unfulfilled.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
We have old age pensions. And as my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said to-night, the reason why we have old age pensions is that the late leader of this group, the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, the then member for Winnipeg North, Mr. Heaps, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) fought for them in this house. One of the treasured possessions of this movement is a framed letter which hangs in our national office, sent by the Prime Minister in 1926 in reply to a query presented to him and to the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was then the leader of the Conservative party, as to what they proposed to do with old age pensions and unemployment insurance. The present Prime Minister gave Mr. Woodsworth the assurance that if'he received the support in this house that would enable him to carry on the government, old age pensions would be introduced at that session and that unemployment insurance would be considered. We have that letter hanging in our national office. The reply of the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen was not as satisfactory and history records what happened. We got unemployment insurance in 1940, years and years after unemployment insurance was overdue in every country of the world; and moreover because I believe the revenue was valuable to the country at that time, the contributions made
by the individual workers to the unemployment insurance fund were to be not only a cushion when the war ended but one means of withdrawing from circulation the wages that would help to reduce the purchasing power of the nation.

A new taxation

With regard to international trade, I am in complete agreement with those who believe-and we all are- that we must have trade between the nations of the world which is to be. But I would point out that the level of world progress is the level of the sum total of the progress of the nations of the world; consequently, my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South is perfectly correct when he says that we ought to be endeavouring to control our own economy in order that we may raise the levels of our own standard of living and thus contribute to the progress and the Welfare of the world.
This bill is to set up another department, a department which will be valuable in the future. But what is that department going to do? It is merely going to coordinate; it is merely going to encourage the production of plans of whom; of individuals, of corporations? Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to-night that unless we are prepared as a nation to integrate our resources, to plan our economy, to plan our economic ventures, if you like, then we shall not achieve the objective which we have, which is full employment.

speechtext:
What I have in mind is this: It is not a department of government which will organize the development of our resources, to plan our economic activities and
Department oj Reconstruction

to carry them out in the interests of the nation. We still have to rely on private enterprise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: No. This is a department to get all of the departments of the government to work on anything and everything that will further reconstruction and development.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Of course; but the government is not going to take steps to see to it that we develop our resources ourselves, and I will give a concrete reason for making that statement. Yesterday this house passed a bill to dispose of certain war assets, certain factories, machines and equipment, when the war ends, giving a group of individuals the power to get rid of these things. That was the representation made by the chamber of commerce to the reconstruction committee. As I recall their brief-and I am speaking entirely from memory, because I did not intend to speak to-night-they urged upon the committee that when the war ends, the equipment we have gathered together should not be allowed to interfere with the normal activities of industry in this country. Three years ago I sat in the war expenditures committee and heard an outstanding leader of industry in this country suggest that we should set up a committee to see to it that these things were disposed of in such a way that they would not interfere with normal business enterprise in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
permit a question, he would not dump that nine billion dollars worth of equipment on the market at one time?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I would not dump it on the market at all. Anything that can be used to develop our resources or to manufacture goods of value to the Canadian people I would have continue to operate under government control, supervision and ownership. That is what I would do with it, but instead it is proposed once more to deliver ourselves and our economy into the hands of the private enterprisers who led us into destruction following the last war and who were responsible for the years of depression through which we went subsequently. It is all very well to say that to-night the government is penitent, that to-night the government intends to turn over a hew leaf and do something in the future; but what is the record of this government? Look back at that record over the years. I remember that in June, 1939, my hon. friends to my immediate left rose in this house and asked that $200,000,000 of money be issued to give work and food and relief to the workers

and farmers. I saw that the house was not going to accept that amount, and I moved an amendment suggesting $100,000,000. What reception did we get? We were told that the budget had just been passed, that we had made a large appropriation for the nation's finances, and that we could not afford another $100,000,000. I was looking up the debate the other day, and I remember saying that if war came in the next two or three months we would not find one hundred million dollars but many hundreds of millions of dollars in order to prosecute that war, and we have had to do that. We shall continue to do it until this war is won; but let me say, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, that what we did in war for destruction we shall have to do for construction when the war is over. Do you mean to tell me that those surrounding the Prime Minister to-day, the orthodox financiers and the orthodox enterprisers, will tolerate an argument of that sort when the war ends? I hear from various sources and I read in the newspapers the continuous demands that even in this budget the excess profits tax must be removed and the income tax reduced, in order that industry may accumulate something for the post-war period. That is the propaganda; that is what the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Essex East and all the others are surrounded with at the present time. I see no disposition on the part of the government in this bill, or in any other bill before this house, to grapple with this basic problem. As my colleague said a few moments ago with regard to conditions before the war, I repeat that a government must be judged, not only by its general philosophy but by its actions in the past, as to the sincerity of its intentions in the future.

I am not aware of any,
except possibly my hon. friend to the left-

The Minister of
Finance (Mr. Ilsley).

I ask my hon. friend if it
is not a fact that it was this government which imposed the excess profits tax and raised the income tax to the highest level ever known in this country. This government, which is supposed to have orthodox financiers as advisers, did that, and my hon. friend should mention that fact to be fair.

Department oj Reconstruction

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I agree that that has been done, under the necessities of war, but I was saying that the whole propaganda at the present time is to remove those taxes in order that industry may proceed in the normal way. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Not a glimmer of intelligence.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: We have to reckon, when this war is over, with a situation which, as the hon. member for Essex East has said, will challenge the intelligence of every hon. member of this house and of every party within it. The boys who are in the armed forces, the boys who are overseas to-day, are not going to come back to the kind of Canada we knew before. I have just been through an election campaign in which the paraphrased slogan of the friends of the government was: "Put the retiring premier back in office to give you the same kind of administration in peace that he gave you before and during the war." No, Mr. Speaker, that is. not what the young men in the armed forces are expecting of us. I am tired of picking up magazines and reading the propaganda they contain; pictures of boys in foxholes saying, "Gee, I hope Canada will be the same kind of Canada that I left." I say quite reverently, God forbid it. That was the kind of Canada we had under this government from 1935 to 1939, the kind of Canada we had under the preceding government from 1930 to 1935, when boys asking for bread were giving tear-gas bombs; when boys who were in this city in February, 1939, asking for bread were described in this house by members of parliament as yaps, as ne'er-do-wells, and as spineless.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
That kind of thing has to stop, and what I fear in this bill is that we have another paper organization which will not do anything about it. On behalf of those associated with me, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that there is no possibility of full employment; there is no possibility of doing what- I believe the Prime Minister wishes to do, and at the some time maintain the profit and free enterprise system. To-night we have heard a great deal about New Zealand from my hon. friends to my left. The hon.
member for Essex East knows what that country has done. He knows that the gentleman who was made president of the I.L.O., Mr. Nash, was elected largely as an appreciation not only of what he had done but also of the leadership his little country has given in the realm of social and economic reform.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: But it is not a socialist government; it is not a government of socialism.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Is it not? It is a socialist government, and you cannot tell Mr. Nash that it is not. Of course it is a democratic socialist government, just as we ourselves believe in democratic socialism. Do not tell the New Zealanders that they are not socialists; they simply will not believe you. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that this falls far short of what is expected of the government at this time. I should like to see a plan produced under which we could use this 8800,000,000 worth of machines and equipment for which this nation has paid during the war. I should like to see a thorough attempt made to develop the resources of this country, and to prepare plans for their development in the public interest.
Why, when we look across this country to-day and see what is waiting to be done, and no plans to do it-

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

No.
Department of Reconstruction

A land settlement

That in order to effect
those changes it would be necessary to have a system of public investment in private enterprise, with private initiative, and I wished
the government to maintain a measure of control by which that could be sustained.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I did not even mention the word "regimentation".

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: No, I know the hon. member did not. But that is the interpretation placed upon the controls. People across this country are criticizing these controls. If we are to have controls-and undoubtedly we shall have to have some controls-let them be democratic controls, not the controls of the kind we have to-day, with dollar a year men at the top assuming the responsibility in connection with these controls, men appointed by order in council. Let us have controls through the democratic organization of the people's representatives. That is something we do not have have to-day.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: That is our policy.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
But, sir, what I really rose to say was this, that in spite of all the fine words we have heard-and we have heard them before; we heard them in war time before, and we heard them for a second time to-night-we want to see some action. We want action, rather than words. If there is no action, then we face a period of great difficulty. We face a period of chaos.
I do not wish to see chaos. Rather, I wish to see orderly progress. But that kind of policy which the government has pursued in the past, and is pursuing to-day, does not give me much hope that we shall emerge into an era of peace within our country, or an era of prosperity for the common man. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government in setting up this department will go far beyond what they are prepared to go to-night, and will see to it that the great enterprises which we have built up during this war for the people of Canada are preserved and are used by the nation to give opportunities of life and of work to the great masses of people in this country.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member when he was speaking. However, he did make reference to a plan. I would point out that there has been a major plan in connection with complete town planning for Toronto. I know the town planning

Department oj Reconstruction
organization has worked on it for three years, and it has been accepted, and is on view in Toronto.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I was thinking of a plan for the whole country. A plan for all Canada would be more fitting than that. However, I do appreciate, of course, what Toronto has done.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my point of view with respect to this bill is different from that expressed by most hon. members to whom I have listened to-night. I took a great deal of interest in many of the proposals presented to the parliamentary committee on reconstruction, and while I found many of them were provincial in character, a large number were national in scope.
Those briefs presented by provincial governments, which had been prepared by departments of public works, departments of agriculture and departments of lands, mines and forests in the provinces, were national in outlook. Also the briefs prepared and presented by the associations of engineers and architects were national in their outlook.
To-day we have heard hon. members discuss labour problems in connection with this bill. However, I believe that discussion might better be had under the Department of Labour than under the Department of Reconstruction. We have heard the statement that the prosperity of the country depends upon the prosperity of the primary industries. That is true. However, that has been taken care of by a guarantee of a price floor on products of the farms and fisheries.
One hon. member mentioned that the success of our country after the war depends upon our exports. Here again, in my view this depends upon the Department of Trade and Commerce. As I view the bill, it would be my opinion that it should have been called, "An Act to Establish a Department of Reestablishment and National Development." I have hopes that this new department will develop into a department of national development.
It appears to me that the development of Canada, so far as national development by the federal government is concerned, stopped about thirty years ago with the completion of the railways and canals construction in the country. I feel that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should appoint an able man at the head of this new department, one who has a wide national outlook. He should have as his assistant an able man to plan what should be done by the departments. In my view, plans should be prepared for a wide national development. ' In the first place, I
feel that we need several more transcontinental highways, running from coast to coast, and I believe that it is the duty of the national government to provide them. This should be completed in the interests of the devolpment of this country. Lateral highways paralleling the Alaska highway should be extended to the north for the development of all that section in the west, because it certainly cannot be regarded as a provincial obligation. Then there are the flood controls of our great rivers. We have just had a report of a disastrous flood in the northwest territories. This danger will increase as the country becomes more settled, until the yearly damage will run into millions of dollars. In the United States, where more development has taken place, flood damage every year amounts to billions of dollars. The problem is a national one and should be dealt with by this department from the viewpoint of national development.
There is also the matter of protecting our forests. Our federal government derives large amounts of revenue from forests in the various provinces, and it is in duty bound to assist, by building roads and patrolling, to provide fire protection in all the forest areas. The development of our airways must also be undertaken.
As I visualize this department, it will be a permanent organization and over the years will spend billions of dollars on national development. I look upon it as providing the means in conjunction with the Bank of Canada to control and stabilize national income and national employment. If a scheme is prepared envisaging expenditures upon development to the extent of several billions of dollars over the next few years, then, as private enterprise is unable to provide employment, the wheels of progress can be put into action by this development to give employment and raise the national income. So long as private enterprise is able through the demand for its products to stabilize the national income, the department's work can be tapered off; when the demand for the products of private enterprise diminishes, this department can take up the slack by proceeding with a great programme of national development. The one thing necessary is that the minister as the head of the department shall not lose sight of the object for which it is created and must not go on with his development programme when full employment is otherwise available and provided.
Immediately after the war, I assume, the piled-up demand for civilian goods will allow private enterprise to supply all the employment which is called for in the early years.
Department of Reconstruction

When that demand is satisfied the department must come in and take up the slack and build up the national income, and do it on a uniform basis. If, as I have said, the department is properly administered it can, along with the Bank of Canada, iron out the high spots in our national economy and smooth out the low spots, so as to maintain a good average national income with steady employment. If whoever is in charge of this department takes that point of view he will have an opportunity of taking care of any depression which we may run into immediately after the war, and, indeed, for many years afterwards, and can foster, over the years, a steady progress which will protect us against periods of depression and avoid periods of excessive employment.
I would urge upon the Prime Minister that this department be established as soon as possible. We know to-day that with the impact of mechanized equipment, powerful armies fade away in a very short time. This war may come to an end very quickly through the collapse of the German army, and we shall then need this department to take care of the difficulties in the immediate post-war period. Unless whoever takes charge has at least six or eight months in which to prepare his plans and to gather around him an able body of administrative assistants, we shall again be facing what we were confronted with in the first year of the war, when we were not at all prepared, and floundered around without getting any results.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
It was not my intention to speak on this matter to-night, but I have been prompted to do so because of what has been said by some hon. members with regard to the setting up of this new department. I should first like to draw the attention of the house to the comment made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) in trying to chastise the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for having been somewhat slow and cautious in bringing down these reforms. I think I have heard speakers of the C.C.F. admit, in exposing their particular philosophy, that it will be some time before they will be able to implement their "pie in the sky'' for the people of Canada. After all, even twenty years is not long in the lifetime of a nation, and far more progress has been made in this country under the leadership of our present Prime Minister in the matter of advanced social legislation than has been made in any previous time; also it will compare favourably with that of any other country.
In passing, I would suggest that we try to get a proper perspective in relation to some of the arguments of the C.C.F., because if we

take them in their literal sense they are somewhat misleading. The leader of their party to-night was emphasizing the advanced position of New Zealand in social legislation. It depends upon what measuring stick we apply to advancement. I do not believe Canada needs to take second place to New Zealand as regards high standards of living. I have acquaintances in New Zealand and have asked them about this, and I know that their standard of living is not comparable with that of Canadians.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: From the health point of view?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I am not in a position to tell you how many automobiles there are in New Zealand. I have the record in my desk.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: Have you the health record?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: I know, speaking of Canada, that in Ontario, every fifth person drives either a truck or an automobile. You could load on these vehicles every person in the province, and you would need to put only five in each vehicle and they could all get out in one procession.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext: It might be a good idea.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO FORMULATE AND CARRY OUT RECONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
I believe that to get the same result in New Zealand you would have to put twenty-one persons in each car. Of course it does not follow that the automobile is the only measuring rod of standards of living, but undoubtedly it indicates the purchasing power of a nation, because it is a product which is highly desirable and much in demand.
I should like to commend to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who wants to bring about fundamental changes, the good old book. Perhaps the best politician in the Bible is King Solomon, whose wisdom is shown in the. Proverbs. The Proverbs show that the people of those days experienced some of the same difficulties that we do. I do not look with such misgivings upon this new world so long as we have human beings in it because, in spite of all our difficulties, we have registered a great deal of progress already.
I am one of those who may be considered to have been born in the horse-and-buggy days, but I should like to say that there are some things in regard to reconstruction which it would be well for us to keep in mind. An old philosopher once said that it may be a good thing to have what money can buy, but that it is a tragedy to lack what money cannot buy. There are many things in this

Department oj Reconstruction
life to contribute to the happiness of people which money cannot buy, if we will only get the right philosophy and the right spirit.
The Prime Minister in his introductory remarks this afternoon said that the government had been successful in enlisting the cooperation of many organizations and of many governments and getting their advice in regard to our reconstruction programme. But I still believe that he overlooked one thing, namely, the spiritual life of our country. Much as I commend the chairman of the reconstruction committee I sometimes wondered if it would not have been better to have before that committee some of the leaders in the spiritual life of our country, to see if they were not in a position to make some contribution to the happiness of society. That is one of the things that should not be overlooked.
I have said that I was born in the horse-and-buggy days when the kerosene lamp was the light of the home and the rag carpet adorned the living room floor, when we had three square meals a day and gave thanks to the Almighty for them. The day's work was preceded by reading a chapter of the Scriptures, followed by a supplication to the Almighty for guidance and direction during the day. I would say to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. that when that supplication was made to the Almighty we always gave thanks for the things we had and were not continually asking for more. I commend that to my hon. friends of the C.C.F., who are feeling more enthusiastic to-day than they did a few short days ago. I would commend that philosophy not only to them but even to the other members of this house. Those were the days in which the mother contributed to the family life and when the whole family would gather around the hearthstone at night. Those were really happy days. I was not brought up to be idle. Idleness was not forced on me. At sixteen years of age I had to do my chores and contribute to the family larder in my own small way. I am not so sure that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) made any impression on me by his argument that a living can be made by working only four hours a day and only four days a week. I wonder what would happen to my poor old cows under that system. What kind of cow can he invent that will go three days without milking? These things run through my mind when I hear that particular philosophy expounded by the C.C.F. across the way.
I read an article' in the Globe and Mail recently about a man by the name of Krugg who said that if a dollar had been invested at the birth of Christ it would be worth so
many billions of dollars to-day by virtue of compound interest and to expend the proceeds we would all have to buy 1,500 Ford cars a year. That is the sort of thing that happens when a man goes all out for mathematics and theory without using common sense. My hon. friends over there have the advantage of a great deal of education, but if I did not have an education myself I would far rather have common sense. You can make any kind of argument on theory. But we have to face facts. I rather enjoyed the attitude which the Prime Minister took when he said that in all this reconstruction expenditure the money must not be expended just for the sake of making work but that we want some results from it. I think the money ought to be expended cautiously so that it will finally bring returns.
When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was condemning the capitalistic system I wondered if he thought of the extremely high standard of living which we enjoy under the capitalistic system. Perhaps we have not gone as far as some would like us to go, but we have gone far from the days of the kerosene lamp until to-day when by pushing a button my whole home is filled with light from Niagara falls. To-day we have radios in our homes. Can the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar tell us how many radios there are in New Zealand? He will find that there are only about half the number there that there are in Canada in proportion to population. We can hear the greatest celebrities on the radio in our homes to-day, and it is always a pleasure to hear our Prime Minister while we are sitting around our own hearthstone. This has been brought about under the capitalistic system and I would commend that to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It is all right for him to argue his philosophy, but it has never been tried out, and if he ever happens to try it out, I should like to have an opportunity of sitting in opposition ten years afterwards and reminding him of some of the great and glorious promises he is making to the people of Canada to-day and of showing the horrible disappointments that had come during his regime.
We may not have all the social security measures that New Zealand has, but we do have wages. Our labouring men are enjoying the highest wages that were ever paid in the history of Canada, and by virtue of that we are having to-day an outbreak of what I call Toryism among the working classes. You make a man wealthy and immediately he becomes a Tory. The labour men to-day are organizing in this country as they never did before and are exerting their influence in
Department oj Reconstruction

politics. It is only another form of Toryism. The Liberal party has always taken the middle of the road course by trying to give to the middle classes the satisfactions of life, and they have been successful. They went down to defeat on reciprocity in 1811, in trying to give to the farmers a market for their products, and went down to defeat again in 1930 when they were fighting against high tariffs and a restricted trade policy. We told the country what would happen if those policies were put into effect and exactly what we prophesied came to pass. I assure hon. gentlemen that the middle of the road course is the course that the people of Canada want to take. If they experiment again as they have done in the past they will experiment only to their sorrow and they will come back to the middle of the road course. The Canadian people are not socialists but individualists. They come in the main from pioneers who never asked governments for help, but who were prepared to stand on their own' feet. This country has been developed' on the principle of free enterprise. It has been developed under what the hon. member sees fit to brand as the capitalistic system, but I challenge him to show any other system that would have registered in the last twenty-five years any achievements parallel to the progress registered under that system.
I should like to have spoken longer, Mr. Speaker, but I have purposely refrained from making some comments on this bill which I thought of putting before the house. However, when the bill is in committee there are one or two things which I shall take occasion then to say.
On motion of Mr. Claxton the debate was adjourned.
